AB.key_differentiator: Plan A's primary estimand is the clean adoption event study that directly answers the question and can be defended to the PM, whereas Plan B leads with a share regressor whose denominator contains the outcome — a mechanically-signed specification it then needs permutation nulls, an invented instrument and a demoted Callaway–Sant'Anna "cross-check" to rescue.
AB.rationale:
Both are serious designs by capable people, and neither is lazy. The decision turns on what each puts first and whether the firm can use the output.

The question is a single-name KPI question: does Kalshi adoption cannibalize DKNG deposits, enough to move sizing on a named short/long. Plan A answers exactly that with the simplest credible design — first Kalshi debit as treatment, matched non-adopters within cohort, stacked event study in dollars per user-month, pre-trends, placebos, and a partial-identification breakdown value so the PM learns how much differential trend would have to exist for the effect to vanish. The headline is a dollar path around adoption that a PM can look at and judge, and the "what would have to be true for this to be wrong" answer is built in: A names the real alternative story (users hitting DraftKings limits or self-excluding and migrating to Kalshi) and tests it three ways — pre-trend F-test, exclusion of adopters already fading in −3..−1, and stratification by whether deposits were already shrinking, both reported. It also handles the mundane thing most likely to fake the result: panel attrition masquerading as churn, with an explicit rule for which outcome headlines if the codings disagree. And it refuses to overclaim — dollars observed, not trades; sports-specific substitution flagged as inference.

Plan B's primary specification is its problem. `K/(K+DK+FD)` puts the outcome in the regressor's denominator, so a negative coefficient is partly definitional. B knows this and says so, but the fix — analytic mechanical null, 1,000 within-user reshuffles, baseline-deflated variant, leave-out share, an IV built from a holdout-fitted affinity times national non-sports Kalshi volume, Arellano–Bond, Driscoll–Kraay — is a lot of machinery to earn back the interpretability that a straightforward adoption event study has for free. Tellingly, B carries the clean estimator (Callaway–Sant'Anna on first Kalshi use vs not-yet-adopters) as a subordinate cross-check and pre-commits to letting it win if the two disagree. If that estimator is the arbiter, it should be the headline. That is inverted sequencing, and it costs a fundamental shop with one engineer and a three-person data team weeks it does not need to spend.

Audience fit reinforces this. A 30-person fundamental fund can evaluate matched adopters, a spend path, and a sensitivity to differential trend. It cannot meaningfully interrogate a Kleibergen–Paap statistic on a constructed affinity instrument, and a PM asked to defend a short on that basis will not.

What Plan B genuinely has and A lacks: two measurement-validity points that are real, not decorative. Kalshi distributed through Robinhood and Webull leaves no Kalshi descriptor, so the identified adopter set is a possibly unrepresentative slice — B proposes to quantify the undercount, A only lists Robinhood in its taxonomy. And DraftKings' own prediction-market launch creates a regime break that contaminates the DK deposit outcome in late cohorts; B verifies dates in filings and cuts the window, A only drops a couple of cohorts as generic robustness. B's wallet-accounting decomposition (cannibalization vs expansion) and its FanDuel symmetry test (category substitution vs brand switching) are also more directly useful to a DKNG thesis than A's secondary wallet-share measures, and converting deposits at explicit hold rates rather than asserting a revenue number is the honest way to reach the KPI. I would graft the broker-attribution check, the launch-date regime cut, and the FanDuel symmetry test onto Plan A on day one.

Given Type I error dominates — a false positive here sizes a real short — A's design is the more defensible one, and it is the one whose failure modes the PM can actually cross-examine.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan B answers the question asked with a matched event-study a fundamental PM can actually read and challenge, while Plan A leads with a regressor that contains its own outcome and then buys its way out with IV, Arellano–Bond, Driscoll–Kraay and permutation machinery this firm cannot evaluate, staff, or defend to an IC.
BA.rationale:
The job is to move sizing on DKNG and survive a PM asking what would have to be true for this to be wrong. That favours the design whose headline number is a directly interpretable dollars-per-adopter-per-month displacement with a raw event-time plot behind it. Plan B delivers exactly that: label descriptors (one week), match adopters to controls within cohort, plot -6..-1 parallel trends, then estimate. It is stoppable halfway and still informative — a flat pre-trend plus a visible post-adoption gap in raw dollars is a 60%-confidence answer a PM can act on before any of the robustness list runs. Its evidence standard is well matched: pre-committed specification, SMD balance thresholds with held-out covariates, joint pre-trend F-test with power against the claimed effect, and Rambachan–Roth-style breakdown M reported honestly (with the nice touch that M=0.5 is declared not a result in advance). Its placebo set is derived from the mechanism rather than recited: grocery/fuel, pseudo-adoption on then-inactive adopters, a comparable-ticket unrelated new merchant, and the whole pipeline run on FanDuel-only non-DraftKings users. The reverse-causality threat that actually matters here — DraftKings limiting or self-excluding a heavy bettor who then wanders to Kalshi — is named and handled with a -3..-1 fade exclusion and stratification, not just listed.

Plan A is the more ambitious study and it is not a bad one. Its two genuine advantages are real: it is the only plan that confronts broker-distributed Kalshi (Robinhood/Webull order flow carries no Kalshi descriptor, so those adopters silently sit in Plan B's control group), and it is the only plan that converts deposit dollars to revenue at explicit hold rates, which is what sizing actually needs. But its core design choice is self-inflicted. Making the primary regressor a within-user share whose denominator contains DraftKings spend builds a mechanical relationship into the estimate, and the entire permutation-null, baseline-deflated, leave-out-share apparatus exists to undo that choice rather than to answer the question. The clean version of the question — did adopters spend less than they otherwise would have — is available and is what Plan A relegates to a Callaway–Sant'Anna 'cross-check.' The tie-break rule (if the elasticity and the ATT disagree by more than 2x, the event study wins) is an admission that the event study was the right primary all along.

Fit compounds this. Three data people and one engineer, no production ML, output going to an investment committee: an IV built from a held-out-fitted affinity score interacted with national Kalshi volume, plus Arellano–Bond, plus Driscoll–Kraay lags, plus ppmlhdfe, plus ten pre-specified splits, is more researcher degrees of freedom and more surface area to defend, and none of it produces conviction with an audience that cannot evaluate it. In a concentrated book where a false positive on cannibalization gets expressed as a short and cannot be diversified away, the defensible-and-inspectable design beats the maximally instrumented one, because the failure mode is a PM unable to interrogate the machinery and either over-trusting or discarding the result.

Neither plan does the incremental-view work — what the sell side already assumes about Kalshi cannibalization of DKNG, and whether a measured displacement would even be news — and Plan A gets a partial credit here for at least mapping deposits to revenue at take rates. That is not enough to overturn the sequencing and firm-fit gap. I would put the analyst on B and graft two things from A onto it before the first run: an explicit measurement of how many Kalshi users are invisible because they trade through a broker, treated as a control-contamination bound rather than an afterthought, and a stated conversion from displaced deposit dollars to DKNG revenue at hold.

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B makes its hard kill depend on an MAU→seats gate whose "seat" variable is itself a ragbag of non-comparable disclosures (pays-per-control, paying users, customer counts, employees-on-platform), so it can foreclose the question actually asked — does MAU predict ARR — on evidence that cannot support that verdict; Plan A tests the asked target directly, with a clean negative control.
AB.rationale: Both plans are competent, over-engineered, and firm-feasible; the choice turns on what each actually delivers to a PM sizing named positions. The question is whether MAU predicts ARR. Plan A tests exactly that: ARR/subscription revenue as a carefully tiered, point-in-time dependent variable (three definitions, never mixed within a series, explicit splice rules), log MAU at h=0,1,2 so there is a genuinely forward-looking read consistent with a 6–18 month book, benchmarked against carry-forward, trailing growth and a no-MAU two-way FE model, gated on rolling-origin and leave-one-company-out rather than the leaky random split it flags itself. Its falsification is the best single test in either plan and is derived from the mechanism: refit on the deliberately excluded consumption-metered names, and if MAU works equally well there, the seat story is measuring something generic and the thesis dies. Plan B's virtues are real — a mechanism gate up front, a kill criterion, the variance decomposition of ARR growth into seats versus price published before model results (cheap and genuinely entropy-reducing), and the sharpest edge test in either plan (regressing consensus surprise on model-minus-consensus). But its primary claim is MAU→seats, not MAU→ARR, and it pre-commits to reporting a negative result rather than falling back to the reduced form the fund actually needs. That kill rests on a gate sample of roughly eight to ten firms whose disclosed quantities are not the same object — ADP pays-per-control, Dropbox paying users, Atlassian customers and tier mix, Dayforce employees on platform — pooled into a single g^seat with four simultaneous thresholds (β in [0.5,1.5], partial correlation ≥0.45, positive in two-thirds of firms, LOO stability). On that N, with that measurement heterogeneity, failure is at least as likely from the gate's own construction as from the hypothesis, and the plan then stops. That is a Type II error dressed as discipline, and it also leaves the firm without the one output it asked for. Plan B is additionally more print-event shaped (nowcast five business days after quarter end) than the stated horizon, and its ridge-plus-empirical-Bayes stack is the part a PM can least interrogate. Plan A's own excesses — CIPS panel unit-root and Westerlund cointegration on ~20 quarters and ~40 clusters are near-powerless, and the horizon is fitted — are cosmetic by comparison, and it keeps a plain log-log FE headline the PM can read. Close, but A answers the question on the right variable with a falsification that can actually fail.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A puts the premise-killing test first — does panel MAU actually track disclosed billable seats, and do seats even drive ARR-growth variance — while Plan B assumes the MAU→seat link and only learns the answer after building the full ARR forecasting stack.
BA.rationale:
The question's hidden premise is that portal MAU measures the billed unit. Plan A tests exactly that, up front, against companies that disclose seat-like counts (pays-per-control, paying users, employees-on-platform, customers × seats), with pre-committed pass thresholds and an explicit refusal to fall back on a MAU-vs-revenue regression if it fails. It then publishes the ARR-growth variance decomposition (seats vs price/mix) before any model results, which can scope the whole idea out cheaply if price and NRR dominate. That is the right entropy-reducing order for a fundamental fund whose PM will ask what would have to be true for this to be wrong: the answer is 'panel MAU tracks contracted seats and seat growth carries ARR growth,' both of which get measured before anything is modelled. It also gets to an actionable read early — a gate result plus a taxonomy of failures is a usable week-four output. Plan A's edge check is also the sharper of the two: regressing realised consensus surprise on model-minus-consensus is a direct test of incremental information rather than just beating analyst dispersion.

Plan B is a competent plan and has one thing A lacks — a clean mechanism-derived negative control (refit on consumption-priced names; equal performance sinks the thesis). But it opens with log-level panel regressions and then reaches for CIPS unit-root, Westerlund cointegration and an ECM to repair the spuriousness it invited, when the differenced/YoY form Plan A leads with is both simpler and the specification it will actually trade. It fits the horizon (h ∈ {0,1,2} plus a joint-lag form) on out-of-sample performance, which adds researcher degrees of freedom on ~40 effective clusters, and it never independently validates the MAU→seat link that its own hypothesis flags as the load-bearing assumption. Its 3% MAPE and 150bp bars are asserted rather than derived, as is 'expect edge in smaller-cap names, decaying.'

Given a concentrated-ish long/short book sizing named positions, Type I error dominates, so Plan A's heavier gate is appropriate rather than excessive. Both plans are close, and Plan A's pooled ridge plus empirical-Bayes shrinkage is machinery this audience will struggle to interrogate, but it is bolted onto a simple OLS gate and a damped-persistence baseline a PM can verify. That is why it wins, not by a wide margin.

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B validates the thing that actually kills the desk — whether a named match is correct — against external ground truth with a calibrated abstain rate, while Plan A spends nearly all its rigor certifying cluster cohesion, a proxy that can be excellent while every name is wrong.
AB.rationale:
The deliverable is a defensible ID→ticker crosswalk, and the stated failure mode is a confident wrong match. That makes match precision the only metric that matters and abstention cheap: an UNKNOWN costs a foregone position, a wrong name costs a sized position in the wrong bank. Plan B is built exactly around that asymmetry — per-ID abstain sink, accept only at max p≥0.80 with margin and ≥3 independent comparators agreeing, thresholds recalibrated to a 95% precision target, coverage (deposit-volume-weighted) as the quantity sacrificed, and a pre-committed kill: if the Netherlands pilot fails, stop; below 40% assigned coverage the country is not identifiable. Its holdout unit is the institution, not the transaction, which is the correct unit for this problem, and the A/B register split with CI enforcement is a real guard against the circularity that would otherwise ruin the work (vendor 'market shares' that are themselves panel-derived, anchors leaking into features). Crucially, several comparators are humanly checkable one at a time — exact cents-level recurring fee matched to a published Preis- und Leistungsverzeichnis, branch/ATM footprint vs NUTS-3 geography, benefit-payment calendars, disclosed neobank growth — so a PM can interrogate any single match end to end and answer 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong.' Controls come first: permuted fingerprints must score at chance, three phantom IDs must abstain, dropping the largest comparator must degrade gracefully. That is a falsifiable design.

Plan A is a technically strong clustering study answering an adjacent question. Its hypotheses are about separation, stability and interpretability of clusters; its gates are silhouette, Hennig bootstrap Jaccard, window ARI and a permutation null. All of that can pass with flying colours while the actual naming — the only step the desk can trade on — rests on a thin, unvalidated final move: rank panel customer counts against market share within a country×archetype cell and run Hungarian on rank distance, accepting when the top-to-runner-up gap clears a preset margin. There is no ground truth anywhere in Plan A, so precision of names is never measured, only asserted; the escalation rule is 'calibrated' against nothing. Worse, the rank-matching assumes the panel's institution shares track market shares, which is precisely the assumption Plan A's own pitfalls section says is violated (young/urban/digital/multi-banked skew inflating neobanks, under-representing Sparkassen and cooperatives) — it names the risk and then proceeds to build the naming step on it, with 'use panel-reweighted shares; state bias' as the whole remedy. Its Tier A output (country + archetype) is honest but unusable: you cannot underwrite a ticker with 'a German savings specialist.' The account-role confound (primary vs secondary vs savings) is a genuinely sharp observation and the strongest thing in Plan A, but Plan B's per-type selection term and post-stratification cover much of the same ground, and B could absorb that check cheaply.

Sequencing and steerability also favour B: a single-country pilot with a stop rule, controls before scoring, and intermediate artefacts a person can inspect (candidate sets, abstain reason codes, type-level confusion, risk–coverage curve). Plan A produces nothing tradable until the whole clustering pipeline has passed its gates, and its most inspectable step — hand-reading 20 customer narratives per cluster — is scheduled last.
issues_with_winner: Heavy build for a three-person data team and one engineer: consented surveys in five countries, OSM Overpass extraction, tariff-document parsing and benefit-calendar logic; the NL-first pilot mitigates this but the plan should explicitly stage the data spend behind the pilot result.

25–60 validation labels per country cannot establish 95% precision with any tightness; the plan should lean harder on the per-match consistency argument (multiple independent comparators agreeing, out-of-time stability across quarters) than on a precision point estimate it cannot support.

Some machinery is unnecessary and unevaluable by this audience — Sinkhorn marginals entropy-matched to a Gibbs sampler, Venn–Abers calibration, leave-one-country-out weight transfer. The Jonker–Volgenant point estimate plus a hand-checkable comparator table would carry most of the conviction; the rest adds researcher degrees of freedom.
Does not test the simplest thing first: exact fee-signature matching alone may resolve a large share of IDs, and that one-page check should precede the full min-cost-flow scoring apparatus.
Does not address the primary/secondary/savings account-role confound that Plan A correctly flags, which can distort n_share, payday and benefit_mix fingerprints.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A validates the thing that actually matters — whether a named match is correct, against external labels, with abstention and a pre-committed precision floor — whereas Plan B's entire validation apparatus measures cluster cohesion and stability, which can be excellent while every name is wrong.
BA.rationale:
The deliverable here is a defensible ID→ticker crosswalk, and the stated failure mode is a confident wrong match feeding position sizing. That makes this a capability build with a hard Type I asymmetry, and the decisive question is: how do you know a match is right, and what abstains when you don't know?

Plan A answers that directly. It builds an external label set (consented survey seeds, provider-revealed IDs, unambiguous public cases), holds out at the institution level (leave-one-institution-out with in-fold refitting, then leave-one-country-out), and pre-commits a criterion in the units the desk cares about — share of panel deposit volume assigned at ≥95% precision, with countries below 40% coverage declared unidentifiable. It ships UNKNOWN as a first-class output with typed reasons, a not-in-roster sink, and margin/comparator-count requirements. It runs the cheap invalidating controls first: permuted fingerprints must score at chance, three phantom IDs must abstain, dropping the largest comparator must degrade gracefully. And it puts a kill gate at the front — if the Netherlands, the easiest concentrated market, fails, stop.

Crucially, A's evidence is the kind a PM can hand-check. "This ID's modal recurring debit is €4.90 to the cent, matching bank X's Preis- und Leistungsverzeichnis; benefit credits arrive on the Kindergeldnummer digit schedule; NUTS-3 footprint matches the branch register" is an argument that survives the question "what would have to be true for this to be wrong?" The register separating anchor variables from feature-building variables, with CI enforcement, is a genuine leakage control on exactly the axis that would inflate apparent accuracy.

Plan B is a well-built clustering study answering an adjacent question. Its gates — silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Hennig bootstrap Jaccard, window ARI, permutation null — all test whether the feature space has structure, not whether names are right. It even says "cohesion isn't correctness" and then proceeds with cohesion as the gating metric. Worse, its naming step rests on rank-ordering panel customer counts against market deposit share within country-archetype cells — that is size matching, precisely the channel most contaminated by the panel skew B itself documents (young, urban, digital, multi-banked, inflating neobanks, under-representing Sparkassen and cooperatives). A confident Tier-B name from that procedure is the exact failure the desk fears, and nothing in B can measure its precision because B has no ground truth at all. Its most likely honest output — country plus archetype — cannot be attached to a ticker, so the plan's realistic success case is not actionable.

B is also mis-ordered for information: NMF co-holding loadings, PageRank on the transfer graph, and UMAP pictures come before any external check that a single ID has been correctly named. A's crude-invalidation-first ordering removes more uncertainty per unit cost.

Against A: the machinery is heavier than this shop's three-person data team and one engineer will comfortably own, and the entropy-matched Sinkhorn / Venn-Abers layer is not obviously necessary before a simpler score-plus-threshold version has failed. But A does pair the sophistication with hand-verifiable corroborators, which is the mitigation the setting calls for, and both plans reach for an assignment algorithm anyway.

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B runs the cheapest disconfirming document test first and produces a priced-in/mispricing verdict the desk can trade, while Plan A front-loads a 40–60 case coded comparable set and Bayesian likelihood-ratio framework that this desk — explicitly with no quant staff and no dataset-building capacity — cannot build and would not use.
AB.rationale:
Both plans are strong on the same core insight: the modal explanation is a pre-agreed release trigger (completion/COD/DSCR), the second-most-likely is substitution of a different form of credit support (keepwell, LC, reserve, take-or-pay, RVG), and the strategic-leverage story only survives if both die with contemporaneous independent qualification evidence. Both pre-register falsifiers. The choice turns on fit and sequencing.

Plan A's methodological centerpiece is a coded sample of 40–60 comparable guarantee releases across semiconductor JVs, digital-infrastructure SPVs and classic project finance, sourced from DealScan, Infralogic/IJGlobal and Bloomberg CACS, converted into a stated prior (20:1–30:1 against H1, ~25x LR required). That is a dataset build for a desk that the brief says consumes sell-side, filings and expert calls and cannot build datasets. It also drifts toward an on-average base-rate question when the desk's stated need is whether this specific situation is mispriced right now. The Bayesian LR framing is also not the language this PM and risk manager will use to size a weeks-to-months catalyst position, and the priors are asserted before the coding that would justify them.

Plan B is ordered for information. The as-signed release language and whether its condition was met is the single test most likely to kill the idea, and it is first. The consent-solicitation/fee check is a genuinely clever near-dispositive discriminator between a negotiated release and a mechanical spring-off, and it is cheap. The VIE maximum-exposure-to-loss QoQ delta is correctly identified as the best test of substituted support rather than removed support. The base rate is scoped proportionately — 5–10 same-vintage sponsor-supported SPVs with shared arrangers and counsel — and reachable through counsel and syndicate calls, which is exactly the desk's real capability. The expert-network chain (deal counsel, lender desk, ex-planners, OSAT/substrate, EDA/IP, rival foundry) with a two-independent-sources rule matches how this shop actually earns conviction, and the requirement that qualification must predate the change respects the 18–36 month timing arrow.

On edge, B asks whether the market already reacted and cross-checks SPV spread against the hyperscaler curve and CDS on both names; A computes economic magnitude but never really asks whether this is already in the price. On output, B ends with a bridge, dated timeline, document-cited verdict and a trade sized to the weakest link, plus the correct trading nuance that dual sourcing is about pricing power and can coexist with rising incumbent volumes. A ends with a chronology and a verdict but no path to a position.

Type I dominates here — concentrated single-name, fast-cutting risk manager — and both set a demanding bar. But B's bar rests on primary documents the desk can actually obtain, whereas A's higher formal bar rests on comparable coding it cannot credibly complete inside the catalyst window, which makes the rigor notional rather than real.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A is built to resolve this one situation on a catalyst clock and ends in a priced, sized trade; Plan B diverts a two-analyst desk into coding 40–60 project-finance comparables to establish an average base rate the desk was not asking about.
BA.rationale:
Both plans read the same way on the core mechanics — they identify the same modal null (scheduled completion/DSCR release), the same accounting null (ASC 810 / VIE maximum-exposure-to-loss), the same substitution null (keepwell, ECL, LC, take-or-pay), and the same independent-corroboration channels (PDK/IP licensing, OSAT and substrate orders, mask/MPW activity, hiring reqs, prepayment lines at the alternative). The tie breaks on fit and sequencing.

Plan A states its order explicitly and conditionally: cheapest disconfirmation first, H1 only entertained if the release-language and substitution hypotheses die, with named killers and an 'any two, no' stop rule. It also puts the one question this desk actually has to answer — is it mispriced now — inside the workflow: check the price reaction first, cross-check SPV spread against the hyperscaler curve at matched tenor and both CDS, and convert the guarantee change into a notional and expected-loss bridge that either shows real risk moved (60–90bp plus funded reserve) or shows the guarantee did little. The consent-solicitation check is close to dispositive and is cheap. The deliverable is a dated timeline, a verdict citing as-signed documents, and a trade sized to the weakest link. That is the output an event-driven PM with a fast risk manager can act on inside weeks.

Plan B is the better-written epistemology paper. Its pre-registered falsifiers are sharp, and it is genuinely stronger on two points: it separates H1 (strategic leverage) from H3 (project souring), which are externally identical and imply opposite trades, and it flags the arrow-of-time problem that foundry decisions precede silicon by years. But its center of gravity is a 40–60 case coded comparables study spanning fab SPVs, data-center ABS/CMBS and power/LNG/toll project finance, plus an eight-quarter portfolio-wide guarantee inventory sweep. That is average-effect work for a desk whose question is always this specific situation, it needs DealScan/Infralogic/IJGlobal, and it is weeks of two-analyst time scheduled largely regardless of what the primary documents say. Worse, it pre-writes the answer the study is meant to produce — 'leverage-driven one to three in fifty, 20:1 to 30:1 against, ~25x LR needed' — an invented base rate and an invented evidentiary bar that will anchor the verdict before a single filing is read. And after all that machinery, B never asks what the market already believes; its pricing section quantifies the risk transferred, not whether the transfer is in the price. Plan A's smaller, targeted base rate (5–10 same-vintage sponsor-supported SPVs, shared arrangers and counsel) is the version of that check proportionate to the decision.

Type I dominates here — concentrated single-name, explicit loss, a risk manager who cuts fast — and A's burden of proof is demanding enough: verbatim as-signed release language, no consent solicitation or fee, exposure-to-loss delta consistent with the released notional, volumes flat or rising, no qualification predating the change. I would take B's H1-versus-H3 discipline as a required addition to A, not as a reason to run B.

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B answers the commercially decisive question — is this residual effect still there and is it already sold by a vendor — in two weeks for near-zero spend, whereas Plan A commits a quarter of annotation and domain-adaptive pretraining before the first return regression and never asks whether the signal is already licensed.
AB.rationale:
Both plans are competent, correctly framed as cross-sectional broad-effect work, and both fit a systematic shop in vocabulary and machinery. The split is sequencing and edge.

The premise here is heavily published (LM 2011, Price et al. 2012) and packaged by at least half a dozen vendors. For a firm judged on crowding, cost and capacity, the first-order question is not 'can we build a better tone measure' but 'is there any residual, uncrowded, post-cost predictability left after SUE, CAR and guidance.' Plan B puts exactly that in front: a frozen pre-registration on day 3, a decay prior anchored to McLean-Pontiff, half a day of vendor calls where availability and client count are themselves read as crowding evidence, then a single LM-dictionary specification and a gate by day 10, with a rank-correlation test against a purchased vendor score that would demote the whole project to 'commodity duplication.' It replicates the 2004-2010 published era as an out-of-time sanity anchor before touching the modern sample, has four pre-committed kill thresholds that include net spread and size-concentration (not just a t-stat), and is genuinely adaptive: pass leads to a build/licence comparison, fail leads to a two-page memo naming residual hypotheses. Stopped halfway it has still taught the firm something.

Plan A is a better-engineered measurement program and a worse research plan. Its economics test — does peer-relative residual tone add anything beyond SUE, announcement return and momentum — is the step most likely to kill the idea, and it sits behind ~2B tokens of domain-adaptive MLM, 6,000 adjudicated gold sentences, 150k silver labels, and a two-head encoder. The LM/FinBERT baselines that could have resolved the question in a week appear as rung one of an ablation ladder run at validation time, i.e. after the spend. It also never asks the crowding question at all: 'break-even cost' is a cost question, not an is-this-already-sold question, and no vendor or published-decay diff appears anywhere. That is a plan that can be flawless and still worth nothing to this firm. Its Cao-Jiang-Wang-Yang machine-readability check and its 'clean null is a real output' line are honest, but a null after a quarter of encoder work is exactly the outcome good sequencing exists to avoid.

Where A genuinely beats B: its cost model (per-share plus TAQ spread plus impact, ADV cap, borrow, capacity where net alpha halves) is real work against B's flat 20bp, and it tests shorter decay horizons closer to the firm's days-to-weeks mandate. But that refinement is post-gate work, and B schedules it explicitly in days 11-14 if the signal survives. I would put an analyst on B and lift A's cost and capacity machinery into that second phase.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A resolves the decisive question — does call tone add anything beyond SUE, announcement reaction and guidance, and has it decayed — in ten days with a pre-committed kill, while Plan B spends a domain-adaptive pretraining run and a 6,000-sentence human annotation project before learning whether any tone measure predicts anything at all.
BA.rationale: Both plans are competent and both are executable at this firm; capability is not the constraint, so the question is order and spend. The literature this question comes from was built on dictionary tone, and McLean-Pontiff-style decay is the single most likely reason the idea fails here. Plan A puts exactly that at the front: a frozen pre-registration, one specification, an incremental-to-SUE/CAR/guidance test, a 2004-2010 replication to estimate the decay curve directly, and four pre-committed kill thresholds — reachable in two weeks at near-zero marginal cost. It also does the one thing this firm's stated criteria demand and Plan B never does: it diffs against what is already sold. Vendor seat costs, client counts, and a one-month trial with a rank-correlation threshold above which the vendor score becomes the control is a direct, cheap crowding test on a signal family that ten vendors already commercialize. Plan A's handling of LLM look-ahead (models trained through 2024 have read the outcomes, so LLM variants sit outside the gate) is the sharper treatment of a risk that is fatal to this specific question. Plan B is the better-engineered version of step two. Its cost stack (per-share, half-spread, impact, ADV cap, Markit borrow, break-even bp, capacity where alpha halves) and its split-sample discipline are genuinely superior to A's flat 20bp and deferred capacity work, and its model-quality diagnostics (gold F1, reliability, ECE, sector-year stability) are the right way to validate a learned tone measure. But the ordering is backwards: LM and FinBERT appear only as rungs on an ablation ladder run after ~2B tokens of continued pretraining and weeks of scarce human annotation. If the LM-tone residual carries no incremental information after SUE and the announcement return, none of that spend was needed, and B has no early gate that would find out. Human attention is the binding constraint here, and B commits the most of it earliest. B is also silent on whether anyone else already sells this score, treating break-even cost as its crowding answer, which is not the same thing. On Type II risk I side with A anyway: it is honest that a dictionary null leaves residual hypotheses (audio channel, LLM variants) and names them in the negative memo, which is precisely the mandate to escalate to Plan B's machinery with evidence rather than on spec.
issues_with_winner: Flat 20bp round-trip cost is crude for a firm with tick data and in-house execution; no borrow, short-leg feasibility, impact model or capacity work until after the gate passes

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B answers the question actually asked — the size of the peer-relative re-rating elasticity to revenue and EBITDA CAGR revisions, cut by industry, in turns of multiple a PM can apply to a named position — while Plan A demotes that to a pass/fail gate and spends its effort on regime instability and market-efficiency questions using machinery this fund cannot evaluate or, in the case of TAQ, even access.
AB.rationale:
Both analysts spot the same real trap (the revised estimate sits in the forward-multiple denominator) and both fix it credibly: A by holding realized LTM EBITDA fixed, B by decomposing Δlog EV = Δlog EBITDA + Δlog multiple as an identity and headlining the EV leg. A's fix is slightly cleaner conceptually; B's is transparent and doubles as a pipeline check. So circularity does not decide it.

What decides it is what each plan delivers and to whom. The firm is a fundamental long/short with a 6–18 month horizon whose output must change sizing on named companies and survive a PM asking what would have to be true for it to be wrong. B produces exactly that: an elasticity reported in %/100bp and in turns at the industry median multiple, a separate loading on revenue versus EBITDA revisions (the question explicitly asks about both), empirical-Bayes-shrunk industry-level elasticities with a rank-stability test that decides whether to pool, and a dispersion interaction. Every one of those is a lever a sector analyst can apply to a specific name where the fund already holds a variant forecast — the edge stays with the fund's own estimates and this study supplies the translation from forecast delta to expected re-rating. The methods (sub-industry×quarter FE, two-way clustering, Driscoll-Kraay, EB shrinkage) are within reach of a three-person data team and defensible in a meeting. B also gives the PM two independent gut checks: the elasticity must land at 25–50% of a stated DCF-implied value (above that flags a pipeline error, which is a genuine falsifier), and a within-industry quintile sort run out-of-sample from 2012.

Plan A reads as though written for a quant shop. Its two stated primary hypotheses are that β is regime-unstable and that the initial re-rating is inefficient; the question as asked becomes a first-stage threshold. Regime instability of a re-rating coefficient across VIX terciles, established via Bai-Perron sup-F, a Kalman-filtered β path, and a variance-ratio-plus-block-bootstrap decision rule, is not something this PM will underwrite or size on. Worse, the identification leans on I/B/E/S detail activation timestamps and a TAQ two-hour signed-return check — the brief says explicitly no tick data. That is a plan step this firm cannot run. Its industry gate (SD ≥ 75bp, median |Δ| ≥ 25bp, ≥50% of firm-months, in ≥60% of months) is a stack of arbitrary thresholds dressed as pre-commitment, and it may exclude precisely the sectors the fund covers without any diagnostic of what was lost. A also never asks the most decision-relevant cut for a sector-organized fundamental fund: where the effect is large and where it is not.

A does have real virtues B lacks — an explicit feasibility gate and stop rule up front, a cleaner off-cycle identification, and the underreaction test (H2), which is genuinely the tradable question for a 6–18 month book. If B is put on the desk I would graft A's H0 feasibility screen and its drift test onto it as a second phase. But B is the plan I can staff, that a PM can interrogate, and that produces a number an analyst can carry into a name. A is the plan that answers a question nobody at this firm asked, with tools nobody there can check, partly on data they do not have.
issues_with_winner: Scope creep in the data ask: Russell 3000 plus MSCI World developed ex-US with Worldscope balance-sheet items, and Visible Alpha 'preferred' for EBITDA, before a cheap US-only pass has shown the effect exists — the US/ex-US split should be a later robustness step, not a day-one universe.

No explicit kill criterion or early stop; the plan is closer to a comprehensive single pass plus a large robustness grid than an adaptive sequence, and the robustness grid (alt DVs, three horizons, FE granularity, crisis windows, ex-2019, contributor cutoffs) is more researcher degrees of freedom than the question needs.
DV still carries an estimated NTM EBITDA denominator; the identity decomposition mitigates but does not fully break the shared-tape problem the way A's fixed realized-LTM denominator does.
H4's list of high-elasticity industries (software, semis, tools, medtech) is asserted as prior rather than derived, and the EB shrinkage will partly manufacture the ordering it predicts.
Dispersion-test endogeneity from news volume is named and then explicitly left unresolved — honest, but it means H3 will not be conclusive.

Timing/predictive version (month-t revision, t+1 multiple) is buried in validation; for a 6–18 month book it is closer to the money question than the contemporaneous elasticity and deserves earlier placement.
issues_with_loser: Relies on a TAQ intraday reverse-causality check; the firm explicitly has no tick data or execution infrastructure.

Primary hypotheses (regime instability, over/underreaction) reframe the assignment; the elasticity actually asked about is demoted to a pass/fail gate, and revenue-versus-EBITDA weighting — half the question — is never a hypothesis.

Bai-Perron sup-F, Kalman-filtered β path, variance-ratio decision rule, stationary block bootstrap, 2SLS on fitted initial re-rating: none of this can be evaluated by a three-person data team or defended to a fundamental PM, and it is paired with no simple corroborating check the audience can verify.
The industry gate is a stack of arbitrary thresholds (75bp/25bp/50%/60%) presented as pre-commitment, with no reporting of which sectors it removes or whether the fund covers them.
No industry-level heterogeneity — the single most decision-relevant cut for a sector-organized fundamental fund — and no output expressed in turns of multiple for a named company.

t>5 as a first-stage pass gate plus Benjamini-Hochberg across regime interactions is a burden of proof calibrated to a systematic factor library, not to a study whose purpose is to modulate sizing on names the fund already researches.

Off-cycle restriction discards 60–70% of events for identification cleanliness; defensible, but combined with the ≥8-peer, ≥3-broker, same-analyst-set filters the surviving sample may be small and unrepresentative of the names the fund trades, and the plan does not report expected event counts.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A answers the question actually asked — how much peer-relative multiple moves per 100bp of 2-year growth revision, by industry, in a form a fundamental PM can apply to a named position — while Plan B silently substitutes two different questions (is β regime-unstable, is the initial reaction efficient) and requires TAQ data and time-series-break machinery this firm neither has nor can evaluate.
BA.rationale:
The ask is a mechanism/valuation-elasticity question whose output changes sizing on named companies over 6–18 months, defensible to a PM who wants to know what would have to be true for it to be wrong. Plan A delivers exactly that: a within-sub-industry-quarter elasticity in %/100bp, industry-level heterogeneity (shrunk, with rank-stability check), an explicit resolution of the shared-EBITDA-tape circularity via the Δlog EV / Δlog EBITDA / Δmultiple identity, a placebo peer reassignment and pre-trend test that can actually fail, and an anchoring of the measured elasticity against a DCF-implied one — an external gut-check a fundamental PM can reason about. Every piece is runnable by a three-person data team on I/B/E/S plus Compustat.

Plan B is the better-written paper and the worse plan for this firm. Its diagnosis of circularity is sharp and its LTM-denominator fix is arguably cleaner than A's, and its H0 feasibility gate and first-stage kill threshold are genuinely good sequencing. But it then reframes the question: the two 'primary' hypotheses are regime instability of β and market over/underreaction. Those are interesting, and the drift branch is even horizon-relevant, but they presuppose the elasticity the question actually asked about and relegate it to a gate. Worse, the identification is a (−1,+1) CAR around single-broker revisions on off-cycle days — a three-day announcement proxy for a 6–18 month re-rating, deliberately excluding 60–70% of events including the earnings-day revisions that matter most to a fundamental book. It then demands t>5 and 20bp/100bp to proceed, thresholds invented rather than derived, which risks killing a real but noisy effect. And the machinery — Bai-Perron sup-F, Kalman-filtered β paths, variance ratios, block bootstraps, 2SLS on fitted initial re-rating, BH correction, plus a TAQ reverse-causality check on tick data this fund explicitly does not have — is unbuildable here and unevaluable by the audience. A conclusion resting on a Kalman β path is not something a PM can defend in an IC.

A is not without cost: it is a large simultaneous grid with no explicit stop/kill point and little adaptivity, and it never asks whether this elasticity is already common knowledge. But its out-of-sample quintile sort from 2012 and its industry-by-industry elasticities give the PM something actionable within weeks, in units he can apply to a name, with named ways to be wrong.

AB.key_differentiator: Plan A puts the idea-killing question — is the public channel-check thesis already in consensus and price, and does this CFO ever raise the full year at this quarter — first and gates on it, while Plan B buries the same cheap kill behind weeks of bottom-up revenue reconstruction, ramp-curve fitting and Monte Carlo that this desk has no staff to build or defend.
AB.rationale:
The information is public sell-side commentary, so the only edge available is a variant view on whether management converts it into a guide raise and whether that is priced. Plan A is built exactly around that: information-date dating, consensus revision and whisper-versus-stale-consensus, comp-relative CAR, implied-fundamentals arithmetic (logos x defensible ACV x in-year landing fraction) versus what the move already embeds, with an explicit two-of-three gate and a written pass note if it fails. Only then does it spend time on the thing that actually determines the catalyst — the CFO's revealed guidance policy at this specific fiscal quarter, the raise-to-beat pass-through ratio, and whether signature-to-recognition lag even lets new logos reach the full-year guide. That is entropy-reducing order for a weeks-to-months event trade, and it can be stopped after a few days having taught the PM something. Its default is 'no' with three of four outcome states bad, which is the right burden of proof for a concentrated book with a fast-cutting risk manager where a false positive is an explicit loss that cannot be diversified away. It also flags the expert-network MNPI issue, which matters at a multi-manager platform.

Plan B contains genuinely better fundamental craft in places — expert calls specified by role including a share-loser, services/implementation headcount leading claimed bookings, new-logo ARR per ramped rep against its own distribution, cRPO cross-check. But it is written for a firm with a modeling team. Reconstructing twelve quarters of revenue bottom-up to within 1%, fitting a ramp curve R(k) by least squares seeded off an S-1 cohort chart, and running a Monte Carlo over four parameters is a lot of machinery whose output nobody on a one-PM, two-analyst desk can audit or defend to the IC, and it adds large researcher degrees of freedom to a number (FY revenue in bps versus midpoint) that the guidance-policy question may render irrelevant. Worse, the check that would render all of it unnecessary — prior-episode channel commentary versus actual raises, and whether the stock already moved — sits at the end under Validation, and is even reported with a pre-filled result (6/8 positive checks, 3/8 raises) as though already known. Plan B also asserts economics its work does not produce: a ~12% downside scenario, a 4% NAV position, an 8% stop, all fixed before any of the analysis has run.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan B puts the cheapest idea-killer — is the channel-check thesis already in consensus and price, and does this CFO ever raise the full year at this quarter — in front as an explicit gate, using tools this desk actually owns; Plan A does the same tests but buries them behind a Monte Carlo revenue reconstruction the desk cannot staff or defend.
BA.rationale: The question is a single-name catalyst call for a desk with one PM, two analysts, no quant staff, and a risk manager who cuts fast. Two things decide the trade: (1) the checks are already public in sell-side notes, so what is left to earn, and (2) whether management's guidance policy at this point in the fiscal year even permits a raise big enough to matter. Plan B makes exactly those two things the gates, in that order, with pre-committed stop thresholds and a written pass note as an acceptable outcome. Stage one is days of work on vendor consensus, revision timing, a comp-relative CAR, and a back-of-envelope logo x ACV x in-year fraction sanity check against what the CAR already implies. That is a 60%-confidence answer fast, and it can kill the trade before any expensive work is sunk. Stage two is transcript and 8-K archaeology on guidance philosophy and raise-to-beat pass-through — precisely this desk's native competence — and it refuses to size until EV is established. Plan A contains the single sharpest test in either plan (the eight-prior-print map of channel commentary to actual guidance action, with an explicit 'stop' if positive checks rarely produce raises), but it sits under Validation, after a full twelve-quarter bottom-up revenue reconstruction tying to 1%, a fitted ramp curve with an invented functional form (R(0) = max(0,(45-L)/90), justified by nothing), a least-squares fit of lag and expansion path, and a Monte Carlo. That is a quant shop's plan dropped on a desk with no quantitative research staff: nobody there can evaluate or maintain it, and it produces false precision — p10/50/90 on full-year revenue in basis points whose inputs are expert-call estimates of registration-to-close rates. The pre-committed gate (>=75bps above midpoint, >=50bps above consensus) then hangs off that fabricated distribution, and the 12% downside scenario and resulting 4% NAV size are asserted rather than derived. Plan A does credit the priced-in problem, but as a late cross-check rather than the gate; B makes the incremental-edge question the whole of stage one. Plan A's edge is its primary-source count work — the desk's real comparative advantage — and B is thinner there; that is the main reason this is not a blowout. But Plan B is adaptive (explicit stop-vs-continue branches), stoppable halfway with something learned, correctly defaults to no in a Type-I-dominant concentrated book, engages the other side (analysts who did not raise, the reverse-sandbag trap), flags the MNPI exposure that platform compliance would actually care about, and reports the small-N base rate as wide rather than dressing it up. Better sequenced, better fit, and no invented economics.

AB.key_differentiator: The question asks whether round-lot flow is profitable to trade against; A answers both the identification premise and the money question on the firm's own terms (net-of-cost alpha, capacity, incremental to published retail-imbalance and short-term reversal), whereas B hard-stops before any profitability test behind a conjunction of five arbitrary identification thresholds that would discard a tradeable signal for failing a recall or label-correlation gate that has no economic content.
AB.rationale:
Plan B is the better-sequenced document in the abstract: it starts with a free spreadsheet test (Rule 605 wholesaler buckets, FINRA MPID) that can kill the premise in a week, and its mechanism tests — price-elasticity of round-lot frequency, round-notional versus round-share clustering — are the sharpest measure-validity work in either plan. If the question had been 'can we identify retail flow at all,' B wins outright.

But the question as asked is whether round-lot flow is profitable to trade against, and the firm's stated criteria are net-of-cost survival, capacity, and crowding. B explicitly refuses to touch any of that in Phase 1 and gates the whole project on identification purity: kill if lift <2x, kill if recall <35%, kill if mean stock-day correlation with a benchmark it itself describes as having 'sign-error rates in the tens of percent' falls below 0.40. Those thresholds are pre-registered, which is good practice, but they are not the firm's decision criterion, and requiring all five to pass simultaneously in a single partition against deliberately noisy labels is a very high Type II rate. For a 200-researcher systematic shop with a replication committee that independently re-runs anything before it trades, the expensive error is discarding a real days-to-weeks signal, not letting a marginal one through. A round-lot imbalance signal that is only partly retail in origin but earns net alpha with capacity is exactly the thing this firm wants to know about, and B's hard stop throws it away by construction while calling that a 'well-evidenced negative result.'

Plan A is not the naive version B caricatures. It treats retail origination as a testable proxy rather than an assumption, and its decisive test is the right one and comes before the expensive machinery: does RLOIB carry an incremental Fama-MacBeth coefficient after controlling for all-lot imbalance and the standard sub-penny retail imbalance? That single test simultaneously handles the mechanism question ('is the lot filter adding anything beyond generic OFI?') and the edge question ('is this just the published BJZZ retail-imbalance signal, or short-term reversal relabeled?'), with day-t return and the STR factor declared non-negotiable controls. It states both failure modes explicitly — nothing incremental, versus real but unharvestable — and makes breakeven cost a headline output rather than asserting a Sharpe. Horizons (1/5/20 day, 5-day holding) match the firm's book; the cost model, borrow fees, participation caps and $50M–$5B capacity sweep are exactly what this committee will ask for; the 2019 split and Q1 2021 stress test are the right regime cuts. The data build is a normal quarter here.

A's real weaknesses are the sprawling sensitivity grid (researcher degrees of freedom, no correction) and the fact that its retail identification leans on residualization against a sub-penny proxy that degrades badly after the migration to midpoint pricing — B is right about that, and I would graft B's Rule 605 pre-check and RLP-flag validation onto A as a first-week, one-analyst screen before the TAQ build. But that is an amendment to A, not a reason to run B, which spends a full project answering the premise and never reaches the question.

BA.key_differentiator: The question asks whether round-lot flow is profitable to trade against, and Plan B answers exactly that — incremental predictive power over all-lot and published subpenny retail imbalance, net of a real cost model, at the firm's days-to-weeks horizon — whereas Plan A pre-commits to stopping before the money question behind five conjunctive identification gates.
BA.rationale: Both plans are microstructure-literate and written for a systematic firm. The difference is what they deliver. Plan A converts a signal question into a mechanism-validation question and hard-stops before Phase 2 unless all five gates pass in a single venue partition. Its motivating worry is legitimate — round-lot imbalance could predict returns mechanically as order-flow imbalance with no retail content — but Plan B disposes of that worry directly and more cheaply by residualizing RLOIB on ALLOIB and ODDOIB and requiring incremental Fama-MacBeth significance over RETOIB (the published BJZZ-style subpenny measure). That single test is both the falsification test and the edge test: if round lots add nothing over the already-known retail proxy, there is no incremental view to trade, and the plan says so and stops. Plan A's gate stack, by contrast, has an arbitrary conjunction (2x lift AND 35% recall AND 70% signing accuracy AND r>0.40 vs a benchmark whose own sign-error rate it concedes is in the tens of percent) that will kill signals whose retail purity is imperfect but whose after-cost economics are fine. For a firm running breadth with an independent replication platform, that Type II rate is the expensive error; Type I is partly absorbed institutionally by the committee re-run. Plan B also matches the firm's decision criteria as stated: survives transaction costs, has capacity. It produces effective-half-spread-plus-square-root-impact economics, a breakeven-cost headline, a $50M–$5B capacity curve, and holding-band turnover control. Plan A's economics are one line of asserted thresholds in a phase that probably never runs. On negative controls Plan B is stronger where it matters: 250–750 mixed lots and exact-100-only buckets are placebos derived from the mechanism, plus a shifted-signal and sign-randomization null; it also pre-commits that a result which is short-term reversal relabeled is a failure, which is the single most likely way this whole idea is spurious and Plan A barely touches. Plan A's real advantages — venue partitioning rather than pooling, the tiered round-lot definition, RLP-flagged executions as near-ground-truth, and the free Rule 605/FINRA spreadsheet check run first as a kill test — are genuine and I would graft the Rule 605 check and the RLP validation onto Plan B as a week-one gate. But those are improvements to a plan, not a reason to choose one that stops short of the question. Plan A's 36-month pre-half-penny window is also oddly thin for a shop where a ten-year intraday build is a normal quarter, and its likely deliverable — 'round lots are not a clean retail marker, here are better identifiers' — is something 200 quant researchers with RLP flags and subpenny classification plausibly already know.

AB.key_differentiator: The question is whether one held-or-considered company's shortage guidance converts into durable revenue, and only Plan A actually interrogates that company's disclosures and compares the answer to what the price already implies — Plan B builds a cross-industry base-rate library this five-person shop cannot source or staff and never returns to the name.
AB.rationale:
Goal first. A company just guided to shortages; a two-PM, two-analyst long-only shop with a three-to-five-year holding period needs to know whether this business's forward revenue is genuinely committed and whether the multiple already reflects it. Plan A answers exactly that: separate RPO from company-defined backlog from announced LTA value (the LTA-to-RPO gap is the right first cut and is cheap), build an agreement register from 8-Ks, IR decks, commitments footnotes and — the strongest single move — the customers' own purchase-obligation tables, which is the closest thing to an external audit of whether the commitment is real. It then closes the loop on edge with a reverse DCF for market-implied versus modeled durable horizon, which is the only place in either plan where 'does anyone already know this' is asked about the actual security. Every input is a filing or a Bloomberg pull; one analyst can do it in Excel, and an IC can inspect each tier assignment line by line. Firm fit is close to exact.

Plan B is the better piece of economics and the worse piece of research for this firm. Its central claim — LTAs are honored in volume and broken in price, and the variable is requalification cost, not contract language, with prepayments funding the capacity that destroys the pricing — is genuinely the thing that would keep this fund from being wrong about the business. It also has the better falsification design: a named falsifier, a held-out auto-semi cycle predicted before checking, and derived negative controls (aerospace/LNG should hold, containers/MLCC should break, ordered by qualification lag not label). But it has misread who is asking. Coding Exhibit 10 contracts across 20-30 episodes in polysilicon, uranium, LNG, containers, ABF substrates and lithium, against TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Argus/ICIS, Drewry/Xeneta, Panjiva bill-of-lading data, SEMI's fab database and PACER/ICC/SIAC/foreign court dockets, is a multi-analyst multi-quarter build with meaningful licence spend, proposed to a shop with no engineers, no database, and occasional dataset purchases. Worse, at the end of it the firm has a probability-weighted haircut and a general framework but no work product on the company in question, no valuation, and nothing an IC can trace to this name. It has answered a question nobody asked, later and more expensively.

The insurance is that Plan A already carries B's key insight in reduced form: it separates quantity coverage from price coverage, states that enforcement damages are an upper bound because suppliers do not sue major customers and renegotiation is the likely outcome absent cash received, notes reflexivity, and requires cash support or real take-or-pay before crediting a commitment. It calibrates haircuts off the 2021-23 semiconductor episode and screens prior shortage cycles. That is roughly 70% of B's economics at 15% of B's cost, on the right security. Type I dominates in a 25-30 position book, and Plan A's demanding, pre-committed thresholds plus explicit disqualifiers (negative implied gross bookings two quarters, channel inventory above 1.5x, a backlog definition change in a quarter that would otherwise have declined, finished goods rising while backlog is called a record) are the right burden of proof — and, unusually, they are the kind of check an analyst can run in week one rather than month three.

Where Plan A is weakest: the numbers are more precise than anything in the plan earns. Tier haircuts of 90-95/70/25-35%, and gates at 60% NTM coverage, 40% year-two, 15% cash support, 20% damages, 45% customer share, two years of horizon, are asserted with a gesture at calibration from a single prior episode. I would make the analyst show the 2021-23 realized conversion arithmetic before those numbers are allowed to gate anything, and I would drop the 10-15 year depreciation schedule and the four-episode backtest unless the LTA-to-RPO gap and the customer mirror-disclosure reconciliation come back ambiguous. Plan A is also a task list rather than an adaptive plan — it does not say which branches die if mirror recovery is below 50% or if almost nothing sits in RPO, which is the point at which the story is over and the rest is unnecessary. That is a fixable sequencing instruction, not a reason to prefer B.

BA.key_differentiator: Plan B answers the actual question about this company using filings a single analyst can work in Excel and an IC can inspect, while Plan A is a 20-30 episode cross-industry base-rate study requiring half a dozen vendor subscriptions and PACER/customs work this five-person shop cannot staff or pay for.
BA.rationale:
The question is single-name and fundamental: a company we may hold for three to five years has guided to shortages and the market is capitalizing that as duration. What the firm needs is a defensible view on whether this company's commitment book is cash-backed and enforceable, and whether the current EV already assumes it. Plan B delivers exactly that: an RPO/backlog/LTA reconciliation from ASC 606 footnotes, an agreement register scored on structural attributes (minimum quantities, indexation, customer cash, take-or-pay damages, reschedulability, RPO inclusion), coverage ratios by segment, customer mirror disclosures as an independent cross-check, and a reverse DCF that states the market-implied durable horizon. Every input is Bloomberg, EDGAR, transcripts and IR decks. A revenue bridge with a tiering table is precisely the artifact a skeptical IC can pick apart line by line, and the pre-committed constructive/negative thresholds make the output judgeable without any pretense of statistical significance the setting could never produce. Its cheapest and most damaging checks - definition drift in the backlog line, finished goods rising while backlog is called record, negative implied gross bookings, cross-supplier double ordering - are exactly the entropy-reducing ones, and any of them alone can kill the thesis in days. It also engages the other side honestly: suppliers do not sue their biggest customers, so damages are an upper bound and renegotiation the base case; reflexivity is named; duration without growth is flagged as a downgrade against a growth multiple.

Plan A is intellectually the better piece of economics. Its core insight - that shortage LTAs are honored in volume and broken in price, and that the discriminating variable is requalification cost rather than contract label - is the mechanism, with a genuine best case (aero forgings, LNG) and worst case (containers, MLCC) and a stated falsifier. But it has been written for a different firm. Coding twenty to thirty episodes' Exhibit 10 contracts, building per-market capacity ledgers, and reconciling against TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Argus, Drewry/Xeneta, Panjiva, SEMI and PACER/Chancery/ICC filings is a multi-analyst quantitative research program with six-plus data licences, committed before any cheap version has been tried. This shop has one analyst, no database, and buys data occasionally. Worse, it drifts from the asked question: the deliverable is a cross-industry base rate and a probability-weighted haircut, with the company's own contracts, RPO trajectory, customer purchase-obligation tables and valuation reached only at the end as a 'live case' with 12-month checks. The step that most cheaply kills or confirms the thesis for this holding - does the company's committed book carry customer cash and appear in RPO, and do customers' own filings mirror it - is buried behind months of historical coding. For a concentrated book where being wrong about the business is what kills you, and where Type I error dominates, the demanding plan is right, but demanding must mean demanding about this business, not exhaustively demanding about twelve other industries.

What I would do is put the analyst on B and steal A's best idea: make requalification lag and second-source fungibility an explicit attribute in the agreement register, and use two or three of A's episodes - not twenty - as the calibration anchor for the tier haircuts. That costs a week and closes B's real gap.

AB.key_differentiator: The question is about one company's margin exposure to a specific licence renewal; Plan A sizes that exposure with filings work one analyst can do and an IC can inspect, while Plan B builds a 40,000-firm-quarter NLP signal research program this five-person shop cannot execute and that never answers the actual question.
AB.rationale: Plan A correctly reframes an unfalsifiable tone observation into the decidable question — how many basis points are actually at stake, with what probability — and puts the killing step first: size the spend. If the licence is 25bps of margin, the whole worry dies in a few days, which is exactly the early kill criterion this setting wants. Everything is sourced from 10-K purchase obligations, material contract exhibits, vendor disclosures and public price schedules — Bloomberg/Excel/filings work, one analyst, and an IC can trace every cell of the sensitivity table. It engages the other side (comparable renewals as a distribution, switching-cost NPV determining where in that distribution the vendor prices), calibrates management's credibility against the prior two or three renewals rather than against tone, and inverts to ask what uplift would actually breach guidance or consensus — which is the decision-relevant number. Type I error dominates for a 25-30 name book held three to five years, and Plan A's demanding standard is the reconciliation and back-test against the last renewal, which is the right kind of rigor here. Plan B is a well-designed plan for a different firm entirely: a systematic shop with engineers, licensed transcript feeds, Visible Alpha, CRSP, pinned LLMs, elastic net, Driscoll-Kraay, Romano-Wolf. It substitutes an easier adjacent target — does evasiveness scoring predict gross-margin surprises across the market — for the asked question, which is about this company's contract. Even if H2 came back positive with t=2.7, it would tell the PM that caginess is on average mildly informative, not whether this renewal costs 30bps or 300bps. Its own stated modal outcome is the null, meaning months of work most likely returns nothing actionable on the name. And nothing in it is inspectable by an IC skeptical of models it cannot audit, nor maintainable by a shop with no engineers or database. Plan A's flaws are real but minor by comparison: contract mechanics are often not publicly filed, so Step 2 may return blanks, and the hypothesis states 30-90bps and 15-30% uplift ranges before any evidence, which risks anchoring. It is also less adaptive than it could be about what happens if the top-down and bottom-up estimates fail to reconcile. But it explicitly handles the case where immateriality is shown and discomfort remains, logging it as a separate open question rather than declaring victory.

Even if executed perfectly, its H2 output is a panel t-statistic, not a view on this company's margins; the single-name work is a footnote ("case-specific" data) buried under the panel.

Firm fit: Plan A requires Capital IQ and StreetEvents transcript licences, Visible Alpha, Compustat, IBES, CRSP, spaCy, pinned embedding and LLM pipelines, 1,000+ hand labels, elastic net, block bootstrap, Driscoll-Kraay, Romano-Wolf. Five people, no engineers, no data scientists, nobody maintaining a database, Bloomberg and Excel. This cannot be built, staffed, or maintained here, and the committee is explicitly skeptical of models it cannot inspect — a deflection classifier with kappa 0.70 is exactly that model. Plan A reads as written for a systematic equity shop that already owns the data plumbing. Plan B is a filings-and-spreadsheet exercise ending in a sensitivity table an IC can read line by line.

Proxy substitution: Plan A takes management tone as the object of study and never tests whether tone maps to this company's margin exposure; it even concedes the modal outcome is that tone is informationless (NDA constraints). Plan B correctly identifies tone as confounded by the negotiation itself, refuses to weight it, and substitutes the measurable quantity that actually drives the answer. That is the right call.

Sequencing and kill criteria: Plan B's Step 1 is the decisive check and comes first — if the licence is a fraction of a point of opex, the question is dead in days and the analyst stops. It pre-commits thresholds (under ~25bps makes tone moot; over ~75bps and unguided forces a call), so the result is judgeable without any t-statistic, which was never available for a single renegotiation anyway. Plan A's decisive test is a strict out-of-sample panel split that arrives at the end of months of pipeline construction and produces nothing actionable on this name at any intermediate point.

Error asymmetry: for a concentrated book, being wrong about the business is the dominant loss. Plan B's evidence standard — top-down/bottom-up reconciliation within 20%, back-test against the prior renewal, adversarial review that the licence is half the assumed size, treating the 75th percentile as median for high-switching-cost customers — is calibrated to that. Plan A's rigor is real but aimed at a hypothesis whose falsification does not protect this position.

Plan B does carry pre-committed magnitude ranges (30-90bps, 15-30% uplift) stated as hypothesis, which is a mild invention-of-economics flag, but they are framed as priors to be tested against the vendor's observed uplift distribution and explicitly overturnable in the single-source step-function case. Plan A also quotes precise bp and lift thresholds it has not yet earned, so this does not separate them.
issues_with_winner: Opening hypothesis states specific magnitudes (mid-single-digit opex share, 15-30% uplift, 30-90bps) before Step 1 measures anything — anchoring risk if the analyst treats these as priors rather than as pre-registered thresholds
Step 2 assumes material-contract exhibits exist; most enterprise licence agreements are never filed, so contract mechanics may be partly unobservable and the analyst should have a stated fallback

Comparable-set uplift distribution from 5-10 renewals is soft evidence with heavy selection (bad deals go unpublicized); the plan flags this but the 75th-percentile-as-median fix is a judgment call, not a correction
Little explicit conditionality between Steps 2-4 — could be tightened to say which steps are skipped if Step 1 shows immateriality
No explicit engagement with why the sell side or management would be wrong about this if the exposure is large and disclosed
issues_with_loser: Answers a cross-sectional signal question, not the single-name margin question that was asked
Requires transcript, Visible Alpha, Compustat, IBES and CRSP licences plus NLP/LLM pipelines and 1,000+ hand labels — unbuildable and unmaintainable by a five-person shop with no engineers
Output is a classifier and panel regression the IC has explicitly said it will not trust because it cannot inspect it
Decisive out-of-sample test arrives at the very end; nothing actionable on the company in question is produced at any midpoint
Concedes the modal outcome is that tone carries no information, meaning the most likely result of months of work is that the premise was empty — worth knowing, but discoverable far more cheaply
Cost is enormous relative to what it unlocks for one position; multiple new data licences committed before any cheap check on this company's licence spend
Case-specific evidence (purchase obligations, Item 1A redlines, vendor filings) is listed but never given a method, weight, or sequence — the actual answer is an afterthought

response.plan_implied_asker: An applied-micro research shop with a clean transaction panel, judged on identification quality rather than on whether the estimate moves a position
response.what_would_falsify: Stated and pre-committed: rejection of the joint pre-trend F-test on beta_-6..beta_-2; a Rambachan-Roth breakdown M below 0.5 (explicitly declared 'not a result'); non-zero effects in the grocery/fuel/e-commerce placebo outcomes; an effect at pseudo-adoption six months early; a measured MDE above 5% of baseline mean spend triggering a widen-or-pool decision rather than a headline. This is a genuine, unusually well-specified falsifier set on the econometric side.

issues.summary: The plan never states what the market already assumes about Kalshi cannibalization, so no result it produces can be classified as investable versus confirmatory.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Prediction-market cannibalization is the single most-discussed bear item on DKNG through 2025; sell-side has published cannibalization scenarios and management has addressed it on calls. A clean, well-identified ATT of, say, -8% on adopter deposits is only actionable if the desk knows whether the street is carrying -2% or -20%. The panel is a genuinely better instrument than survey and app-download work, but the plan stops at estimation and never converts the instrument advantage into a variant view.
issues.what_breaks: The deliverable — an event-study coefficient with a confidence set and a breakdown M — lands on the PM's desk with no reference point. Any number gets narrated into the existing position.
issues.fix: Before estimation, write down the implied substitution rate embedded in current sell-side DKNG models and in management's own framing, and pre-commit to the estimate range that would be a material surprise in each direction. One day of work, and it defines what success means.

issues.summary: The share of DraftKings deposit dollars attributable to users who have adopted (or plausibly will adopt) Kalshi is never measured, yet it is both the power determinant and the cheapest way to kill the trade.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Kalshi's funded user base is small relative to DraftKings' and the eligibility screen is tight (>=2 DK-debit months, >=$50 cumulative in -6..-1, plus balanced -6..+6 coverage). It is entirely possible that qualifying adopters represent under 1% of panel DK dollars, in which case even a -30% ATT is immaterial to DKNG revenue and the whole matching apparatus is wasted effort. The taxonomy week produces this number for free, but the plan does not list it as an output or as a gate.
issues.what_breaks: The methodology section is scheduled to run regardless. Weeks of matching, stacking and robustness work are committed before anyone knows whether the treated population is large enough to matter economically.
issues.fix: Add as the deliverable of week one, immediately after taxonomy: count of qualifying adopters by cohort, their share of panel DK deposit dollars in the pre-period, and the adoption hazard trend by month. Pre-commit a floor below which the study is written up as 'penetration too low to matter, revisit in two quarters' and stopped.

issues.summary: Kalshi adoption is identified from funding-rail descriptors that include crypto on-ramps, and Kalshi-powered event contracts routed through Robinhood are not excluded from the control group.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The taxonomy explicitly lists 'debit-card/crypto on-ramps' under Kalshi. A crypto on-ramp debit is not distinguishable from a general crypto purchase, so this rule will label ordinary crypto speculators as Kalshi adopters — a population with a different DK trajectory. Separately, Robinhood distributes Kalshi-cleared event contracts; those users are treated but appear only as a Robinhood debit, and the control definition ('no in-window Kalshi debit') does not exclude them. Treated units sitting in the control pool bias toward zero; misclassified treated units contaminate the ATT with a crypto-speculator effect.
issues.what_breaks: The treatment indicator in the event-study regression measures something other than 'started trading on Kalshi', which invalidates both the point estimate and the placebo logic built on top of it.
issues.fix: Report adopter counts by descriptor variant in the coverage audit and hand-trace 30 adopter timelines end to end. Run the headline on unambiguous KALSHI-string adopters only, with on-ramp-attributed adopters as a separate reported arm. Add Robinhood in-window debit activity to the control exclusion list, or at minimum report the ATT with and without Robinhood-active controls.

issues.summary: Contemporaneous DraftKings-side shocks that hit exactly at t=0 — account limiting of winning bettors, self-exclusion, state deposit caps — are not distinguished from competitive substitution, and pre-trend tests cannot detect them.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's reverse-causality defenses are all pre-trend based: the F-test on beta_-6..beta_-2, the -3..-1 fade exclusion, and strata on whether deposits were already shrinking. A sharp bettor who gets limited by DK in month 0 and opens Kalshi that same week produces a flat pre-period, a clean parallel trend, and a large negative beta_0..beta_6. This is the leading non-competitive explanation and it survives every test in the plan. It also flips the investment reading: DK restricting sharps is DK's own risk management, not a revenue threat from Kalshi.
