Yet the entropy-reducing test is nearly free: US large caps, I/B/E/S, 2012–2024, a binned scatter of ΔCAGR against Δlog multiple inside industry-quarter buckets, plus twenty-five hand-traced firm-quarters of the constant-horizon FY1/FY2 interpolation to confirm the measure is not tracking EBITDA definitional drift (adjusted vs pre-SBC vs post-IFRS16) rather than growth. Nothing in the plan surfaces the distribution of ΔCAGR, coverage by region and year, or a worked example before the full pipeline runs.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of build and a data licence are committed before anyone knows whether the sign and rough magnitude exist, whether ex-US EBITDA consensus coverage is thick enough to support the FE structure, or whether the regressor is measuring definitional noise. A bad branch cannot be pruned.
issues.fix: Run the two-week US-only version first, with three inspectable outputs: ΔCAGR distribution by year, coverage/missingness by region-year, and twenty-five hand-checked firm-quarters. Gate the ex-US extension and the Visible Alpha licence on the sign appearing and the hand-check passing.

issues.summary: Everything is estimated at a quarterly contemporaneous or one-month-ahead horizon, while the book holds six to eighteen months; nothing tests whether the re-rating persists or reverses over that window.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The output is meant to change position sizing on named companies over six to eighteen months. A QoQ elasticity says the multiple moved with the revision inside the quarter; the monthly predictive version extends that by one month. If a large share of the re-rating unwinds over the following two to four quarters — plausible if the market is treating revisions as transitory, which is the plan's own stated reason for expecting only 2–5%/100bp — the elasticity a PM should apply at an eighteen-month horizon is materially smaller than the headline.
issues.what_breaks: The 'turns at industry median multiple' translation that PMs will actually use is quoted at the wrong horizon and will oversize positions.
issues.fix: Add cumulative Δlog multiple at t+2, t+4 and t+6 quarters on the same ΔCAGR, and report the headline elasticity as a decay path rather than a single number.

issues.summary: The NTM and N2Y EBITDA > 0 screen removes exactly the firms whose multiples re-rate most, and does so in a way correlated with the regressor.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Firms crossing from negative to positive forward EBITDA have the largest positive ΔCAGR by construction and the largest re-ratings, and they are excluded in the quarter before the crossing and included after. The plan's response — checking β1 is not bottom-margin-decile driven — tests the retained tail, not the excluded one. In the sectors H4 predicts the strongest effect (software, life-science tools, medtech) this exclusion removes a large fraction of names, so the industry ranking that H4 lives or dies on is estimated on a truncated sample in precisely those industries.
issues.what_breaks: The industry elasticity ordering (H4) and the headline β1 are both estimated off a sample selected on the outcome-adjacent variable; a real effect concentrated in the crossing cohort is invisible.
issues.fix: Report the count and characteristics of screened-out firm-quarters by industry-year, and rerun the whole design on EV/Sales, where the denominator stays defined through the crossing, as a co-headline rather than a robustness line.

issues.summary: The 25–50%-of-theoretical band is used one-sidedly as a pipeline-error detector, but the theoretical elasticity depends entirely on an unobservable persistence assumption.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A 1pp change in a two-year CAGR affects only years 1–2 of the DCF; the 8–12%/100bp figure comes from assuming the revision extends into the terminal period. That assumption is exactly what H1 says the market does not make. So the benchmark and the object of study are the same unknown, and the rule 'above the band signals pipeline error' creates a one-directional licence to hunt for bugs whenever the answer is inconveniently large.
issues.what_breaks: The economic-validation gate can reject a correct estimate or bless a biased one, and it is the check that would otherwise have caught the outcome-conditioned screen in issue 2.
issues.fix: Recast the DCF anchor as a two-sided range spanning zero-persistence and full-persistence revisions, and pre-commit that a β1 outside that full range — not outside a 25–50% slice of one end — triggers a pipeline audit.

response.overall: Technically this is among the more careful panel designs I have read on the desk: the mechanical shared-EBITDA-tape problem is identified and correctly handled via the EV/EBITDA/multiple identity, H4 supplies a genuine negative-control prediction derived from the mechanism, the placebo and pre-trend tests are real falsifiers, and no P&L figure is invented. Two things stop it. The screen that drops large ΔCAGR observations unless price moved >5% conditions the sample on the dependent variable and will bias β1 upward in the tail that carries the estimate, invisibly to the entire robustness grid. And the plan never says what the desk currently assumes about this elasticity or how the fund would get ahead of a consensus revision, so the most likely outcome is an expensively-built confirmation of what every PM and every sector note already carries. Fix the screen, run the two-week US-only version with hand-checked ΔCAGR before licensing anything, write down the PMs' current turns-per-point as the null, and add the multi-quarter persistence path so the number is quoted at the horizon the book actually holds.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold. The generic 'no stated prior / no decision change' framing is the sort of recitation that can be unearned, but it is anchored to specifics of this plan and desk: H1 benchmarks to a textbook DCF rather than to the desk's implicit turns-per-point rule, the elasticity is never connected to the transaction/web panels that are the fund's only route to forecasting revisions ahead of consensus, and the closing quintile sort is correctly identified as a crowded revision-momentum backtest dressed as validation. A PM asking 'what changes' would take this seriously. Flagged uncertain because the edge argument overlaps the contemporaneity point the reviewer treated as a design flaw rather than an edge flaw.

Not in gold, but a sharp and plan-specific catch: the Pitfalls screen drops |ΔCAGR|>20pp unless there is an earnings event or a >5% price move, and a >5% price move is essentially the dependent variable. That conditions sample inclusion on the outcome in the tail where β1 has most of its leverage, and the robustness grid never varies this filter. This is not a canonical objection recited — it reads the plan's own screening rule.

Not in gold. Legitimate given the stated resourcing (three-person data team, one engineer): a global 2005-present PIT panel spanning I/B/E/S or Visible Alpha, Compustat and Worldscope filing-dated balance-sheet items and 8-digit PIT GICS is a multi-month build with licence spend, while the cheap entropy-reducing test (US large caps, I/B/E/S, binned scatter, hand-traced FY1/FY2 interpolation examples to separate growth from EBITDA definitional drift) is nearly free and absent. Concretely tied to this plan's build, not a generic 'do a pilot' note.

Not in gold. Directly earned from the firm context: the book is six to eighteen months, but every estimate is QoQ contemporaneous or one-month-ahead, and the plan's own rationale for expecting only 2-5%/100bp (revisions partly treated as transitory) implies possible unwind over the following two to four quarters. The 'turns at industry median multiple' translation PMs would actually use is therefore quoted at the wrong horizon. Specific, not boilerplate.

Matches gold blocking#3: the NTM/N2Y EBITDA > 0 screen excludes the firm-quarters with the most violent re-ratings, the exclusion is correlated with the regressor (negative-to-positive crossers have the largest ΔCAGR), and the plan's diagnostic only tests the retained sample.

Not in gold. Legitimately reads the plan's own 'economic validation' gate: the 8-12%/100bp theoretical elasticity depends on assuming the revision persists into the terminal period, which is precisely the persistence question H1 claims to be measuring, so benchmark and object of study share the same unknown. The observation that the 25-50% band is applied one-sidedly (above the band triggers a bug hunt, below does not) is a genuine evidence-standard flaw specific to this plan's validation design.

response.plan_implied_asker: Event-driven single-name desk with terminal/consensus access, trading into a specific print
response.what_would_falsify: Explicit and pre-committed: full-year consensus revenue revision since the information date >~0.5% with recent-updater subset >1% above stale mean; (0,today) comp-adjusted CAR above 1 estimation-window SD and above the CAR arithmetically implied by logo count x ACV x in-year ramp; straddle-implied move >~1.2x trailing 8-quarter realized median. Two of three failing kills the long. Stage two adds the company's own base rate of full-year raises at this fiscal quarter as a second falsifier.

issues.summary: The whole stage-one gate hinges on a reconstructed "information date," and every plausible error in dating it runs toward finding a gap that isn't there.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Channel-check theses on a covered software name circulate through sales coverage and squawk before the note is published; broker portals, ANR and Visible Alpha timestamps show publication, not circulation. The plan measures consensus revision and CAR from info-date minus 5 days. If the true diffusion started three weeks earlier, both the revision measured and the CAR window exclude the move that already happened, the measured "gap" is manufactured, and the gate passes a long that is in fact priced. This is exactly the Type I error this desk cannot diversify away.
issues.what_breaks: Stage-one gate (consensus revision threshold and (0,today) CAR threshold). A late-dated information date understates what is priced and green-lights stage two and a position.
issues.fix: Date the leak from the tape, not from note timestamps: scan 6 months of comp-relative price and volume for the start of abnormal drift/turnover and use the earlier of that and the first note as the information date. Report the gate decision under both dates; if the two dates give opposite verdicts, that disagreement is itself the pass note.

issues.summary: The stage-two expected-value figure is built from a regression of earnings-day CAR on guidance revision size estimated on ~12-16 observations, which will produce a coefficient that is mostly noise but will be used to size the trade.
issues.why_it_applies_here: With 12-16 quarters, most of which are "held guidance," there are only a handful of actual revision events and the regression has no usable precision. Multiplying base rates that the plan itself concedes have wide CIs by a coefficient from n<15 yields an EV number with false precision, and "require materially positive expected value, sized against the straddle" turns that number into a position size.
issues.what_breaks: Stage-two EV gate and sizing. The desk anchors on a number nothing in the design actually supports.
issues.fix: Drop the regression. Tabulate the raw earnings-day comp-adjusted move next to what management did to the guide for each of the 12-16 quarters and read the pattern by eye; state the range of moves for hold vs. raise quarters rather than a fitted slope. If the ranges overlap, say the reaction is not predictable from guidance action alone and that no EV can be computed.

issues.summary: The arithmetic bridge that the CAR gate is measured against (logo count x defensible ACV x in-year fraction) is built from free parameters that can move the gate either way.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan correctly notes checks are an undersized sample with no denominator, then uses that same check-derived logo count, times an assumed ACV, times an assumed ramp fraction, as the benchmark the observed CAR must sit below. A 2x swing in assumed ACV flips the gate. Pre-committing a threshold does not help if the quantity being compared to it is discretionary.
issues.what_breaks: Third leg of the stage-one gate; the comparison of implied fundamentals to arithmetic deliverables.
issues.fix: Bound ACV from disclosure rather than judgment: disclosed revenue or RPO per customer, or the 100k+/1m+ customer cohort counts if given. Pre-commit low/base/high in-year fractions from the RPO-to-revenue lag before looking at the CAR, and show the gate verdict under all three.

issues.summary: The cheapest and most decisive check on this name -- what happened the last few times a check-driven optimism episode ran into a print -- is buried in the validation section instead of being step zero.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This company's own record of prior check episodes directly addresses whether the premise (checks convert into guidance surprise here) has ever held, and it is a day of transcript and price work. If the last three episodes ended in a held guide and a flat or down print, the entire plan is unnecessary. As designed, it sits after the event study and the guidance table are already built.
issues.what_breaks: Ordering: setup and estimation cost is sunk before the premise is tested.
issues.fix: Move it to the front as a half-day pre-gate: identify prior check-driven episodes, record consensus revision, comp-relative move into the print, guidance action, and post-print move. If none converted, write the pass note and stop.

issues.summary: A stage-one failure is treated only as a pass, when for this desk the same finding is a short setup.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own three-of-four-bad outcome map -- checks priced, management policy is to hold the guide, straddle rich -- describes a short into the print, not a no-trade. An event-driven book with a fast-cutting risk manager can express that side, and the work to establish it is already done by stage one.
issues.what_breaks: Nothing analytically; the output is under-used relative to the work spent.
issues.fix: Add one line to the stage-one exit: if consensus has revised up beyond the threshold, CAR exceeds the arithmetic-implied move, and the guidance base rate at this quarter is hold, state the short case and what would invalidate it (prior-quarter raise precedent under this CFO, a segment where new logos are large versus the base).

response.overall: This is a well-constructed plan and well matched to the desk: it puts the kill test first, asks what is left to earn before asking whether the fundamental is real, uses the company's own guidance record rather than an industry base rate, pre-commits thresholds, defaults to no, and corroborates the event study with a plain market model the PM can check himself. The one thing that would produce a confident answer that fails in reality is the information date -- reconstructing it from publication timestamps rather than from the tape biases the priced/not-priced verdict toward a long, which is the error this book cannot absorb. Fix that, replace the n<15 reaction regression with a readable table so the EV isn't given false precision, and move the prior-episode outcome check to the front.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold, but a sharp and plan-specific point: the plan explicitly makes the reconstructed 'information date' the anchor for both the consensus-revision window (info-date minus 5 days) and the CAR windows, and the sources named (broker portals, ANR, Visible Alpha) do timestamp publication rather than sales-coverage circulation. The error is also directional — late dating understates what is priced and green-lights the long — which is the failure mode this desk cares about. Earned, not recited.

Superficially the canonical sample-size objection, but it is earned against this specific design: the plan proposes a regression of earnings-day CAR on guidance revision size fit on 12-16 quarters in which most observations are 'held guidance,' leaving very few revision events, and then feeds that coefficient into an EV number used for sizing against the straddle. The plan concedes wide CIs on base rates but not on the regression, so the point adds something. Not in gold.

Legitimate and specific: the plan uses the same check-derived logo count it elsewhere calls a non-random undersized sample, times an assumed ACV, times an assumed in-year ramp fraction, as the arithmetic benchmark the observed CAR must fall below. A modest swing in ACV flips that leg of the gate. A desk would take this seriously; it is distinct from the gold's complaint about the numeric cutoffs themselves.

Reasonable sequencing critique tailored to this plan and this desk: the plan lists 'check prior check episodes' actual outcomes' under Validation, after the event study and 12-16 quarter guidance table are built. Given a two-analyst team and a weeks-long catalyst horizon, moving the cheapest premise-killing test to step zero is a real efficiency objection, not a generic one.

Not in gold and not a criticism of validity, but a legitimate desk-fit observation: the plan's own outcome map (checks priced, policy is to hold the guide, straddle rich) is a short-into-print setup for an event-driven book with a fast-cutting risk manager, yet stage-one failure only produces a pass note. The evaluator correctly flags severity as secondary and that nothing analytical breaks.

response.plan_implied_asker: A fundamental single-name event desk that has been given a small systematic team's modelling budget
response.what_would_falsify: Explicit and multiple: if in the 8-print history positive channel checks converted to raises only 3/8, stop; if Q2 guide-raise history is ~1.0x simple flow-through, burden shifts against a raise; if modelled FY revenue is <75bps above midpoint or <50bps above consensus, or the raise implied is below 1.5x the median Q2 raise, skip the print; cRPO deceleration, weak logo adds, or falling land value stops the position.

issues.summary: The model's resolution is coarser than the threshold the trade decision is gated on, and the ramp/land parameters that drive the answer are underdetermined by the data used to fit them.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The reconstruction is declared successful when it ties to actual revenue within ~1% (≈100bps), yet the position gate is 'FY revenue ≥75bps above midpoint, ≥50bps above consensus.' The quantity being decided on sits inside the model's own admitted residual. Worse, the ramp curve is an assumed form with invented constants (R(0)≈max(0,(45−L)/90)) and L, the expansion path, and initial land value are fit jointly by least squares to twelve quarters of aggregate revenue — many (L, land, expansion) combinations will tie within 1%, and which one is chosen is exactly what determines in-year sensitivity, i.e. the entire answer. Tying to the same actuals used for fitting is not validation.
issues.what_breaks: The Monte Carlo p10/50/90 in bps is precision the calibration cannot support; the 75bps gate then reads as a coin flip dressed as an estimate, and it sizes a 4% NAV position.
issues.fix: Fit on the first 8 quarters and predict the last 4 out of sample; report the set of (L, land, expansion) combinations that fit equally well and check whether the trade decision flips across that set. If it flips, say the arithmetic cannot decide it and fall back on the historical guide-raise-vs-flow-through record. Alternatively restate the gate in a unit the model can resolve — new-logo delta in dollars vs. the median historical Q2 raise in dollars — rather than in sub-1% revenue bps.

issues.summary: The cheapest and most decisive tests sit behind weeks of bottom-up reconstruction, and the print is upcoming.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Three checks — the 8-print record of positive checks converting to raises, the guided-vs-actual flow-through habit, and whether the stock/whisper already absorbed the notes — need transcripts, a spreadsheet and Visible Alpha, and can be done by one analyst in two or three days. They are also the checks most likely to kill the idea outright. The 12-quarter reconstruction, cohort curve fit and Monte Carlo are the most expensive items and only matter if those three pass. Two analysts covering a live catalyst can lose the window doing them in the stated order.
issues.what_breaks: If the base-rate and priced-in checks fail, the entire modelling effort is sunk cost; if they take too long, the print passes before a view exists.
issues.fix: Week one: base rate, flow-through habit, priced-in check, plus a one-page envelope (logo delta × land ACV × half-year ramp / FY revenue). Only build the reconstruction if the envelope lands in the ambiguous band between the noise floor and the gate.

issues.summary: The designated kill test cannot measure lift as specified — with 6/8 quarters showing positive checks there is almost no contrast.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'Positive checks 6/8 times but raises only 3/8' compares a near-constant conditioning variable to an outcome; 3/8 may simply be this company's unconditional Q2 raise rate, in which case the checks are neither informative nor disconfirmed. Only two negative-check quarters exist, so no conditional comparison is available on this name.
issues.what_breaks: The gate that decides whether the rest of the work happens is mis-specified; it could kill a live setup or wave through a dead one.
issues.fix: Restate the test as a within-event pattern rather than a lift: in each of the 6 positive-check quarters, did the guide move above simple flow-through, and had the whisper/price already moved before the print? Consistency of that pattern across 6 same-name events is real evidence; a 3/8 ratio is not.

issues.summary: An eight-observation regression of post-earnings returns on estimate revisions is used to produce a 1.2x expected-vs-implied gate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Eight post-print observations, spanning at least one multiple regime for a SaaS name, cannot support a fitted slope precise enough to justify a 1.2x threshold on expected move. The gate looks quantitative but the coefficient will be dominated by one or two prints.
issues.what_breaks: Position/no-position and sizing rest on a number with no stability; the risk manager cannot defend it after a loss.
issues.fix: Tabulate the eight events directly — revision size, whisper gap, realized move — and read the relationship by eye. Use the realized-move distribution and the whisper gap as the comparison to implied; drop the fitted coefficient and the 1.2x precision.

issues.summary: The 8% price stop sits inside the event's own move distribution and the 12% downside figure is asserted rather than derived.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan collects front-expiry implied move and realized moves over 8 prints, which for this kind of name are plausibly near or above 8-10%. Holding through the print with an 8% stop means a guide-down gaps through it, so the stop does not bound the loss it is sized off. The ~12% downside scenario that produces the 4% NAV sizing is stated without being traced to either the realized-move distribution or a de-rating scenario on a missed guide.
issues.what_breaks: Sizing is anchored on a loss number the stop cannot enforce; actual loss on the adverse branch is larger than the risk budget contemplates.
issues.fix: Derive downside from the realized down-move distribution across the 8 prints plus a multiple-compression case on a guide-down, and size to survive the gap without relying on the stop — or express the event leg in options, since front-expiry pricing is already being pulled.

issues.summary: Alternative-data stack and 12-quarter reconstruction exceed what a two-analyst desk with no data capacity can run, and the licences are committed before the cheap kill test.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The desk is described as consuming sell-side, filings and expert calls with no capacity to build datasets. HG Insights/Enlyft, G2 velocity, marketplace listings, job-posting headcount series and a fitted cohort model together are a multi-week data build plus paid licences, scheduled alongside 4-6 expert calls and a full modelling exercise, all before the base-rate check that could end the idea.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst attention — the binding constraint into a print — is spent on inputs the desk cannot maintain, and spend is committed ahead of the test that determines whether any of it is needed.
issues.fix: Keep the expert calls (they are the desk's genuine instrument) and one hand-counted alt-data item if the envelope is ambiguous — implementation/PS headcount postings, which speaks directly to the ramp-lag question. Defer paid vendors until after the base-rate and priced-in checks pass.

response.overall: The instincts here are right for this desk: the null is set as 'the print is not the catalyst,' the guidance decision is treated as a management policy call rather than arithmetic, the priced-in question is asked explicitly against whisper rather than printed consensus, and there are real pre-committed stop-work criteria drawn from this company's own eight-print record rather than an industry base rate. The problem is proportion and precision: the bottom-up reconstruction ties to 1% while the trade gate is 75bps, and the ramp/land parameters that produce the answer are fit to the same actuals that supposedly validate them, so the Monte Carlo will hand the PM a false decimal on which 4% of NAV rests. Reorder — base rate, flow-through habit, priced-in check, one-page envelope in week one — and this is probably answered or killed in three days; build the model only if the envelope lands in the ambiguous band, and drop the eight-point return regression and the alt-data licences entirely.

issue_buckets.why: Same concern as blocking#2 (distributional/bps precision unsupportable given how the model is calibrated) and also hits secondary#4 (the 75bps gate as an arbitrary threshold sitting inside the model's own residual).

Not in gold. Specific to this plan: the plan itself designates the 8-print base-rate check as a stop condition yet places it after the 12-quarter reconstruction and Monte Carlo, with a print imminent and two analysts. A desk would take the ordering complaint seriously.

Not in gold and earned from the plan's own numbers: 6/8 positive-check quarters leaves only two contrast observations, so the declared kill test cannot establish lift against the unconditional Q2 raise rate. This is a reading of the stated design, not a recited sample-size complaint.

Substantially the reviewer's secondary#4 point that the thresholds are arbitrary — the 1.2x expected-vs-implied gate rests on an 8-observation regression with no stable slope. Torn because the statistical-instability framing is a distinct argument, but the conclusion is the same unsupported-threshold objection.

Not in gold and specific: an 8% price stop cannot bound loss through an event whose implied/realized single-day move the plan itself gathers and which is plausibly near or above that level, while the 12% downside driving the 4% NAV sizing is asserted rather than derived. Concrete internal inconsistency in the risk section.

Not covered by gold as written (blocking#2 is about statistical precision, not desk capacity). Grounded in the stated firm context — no quant staff, no dataset-building capacity — against a plan that stacks HG Insights/Enlyft, G2 velocity, job-posting series and a fitted cohort model ahead of the cheap kill test.

response.plan_implied_asker: A systematic equity firm with tick data, in-house execution and a replication-based research committee, trading days-to-weeks
response.what_would_falsify: Pre-committed and specific: if RLOIB's incremental Fama-MacBeth coefficient controlling for ALLOIB and RETOIB has |t|<2.0 at h=1,5,20, the lot filter adds nothing and the idea dies; if it survives but net-of-cost long-short alpha has t<2.0 under base costs, the effect is declared real but unharvestable. Placebos (mixed-lot buckets, forward-shifted signal, within-day sign randomization) must come back null.

issues.summary: The single cheapest kill — how much independent variation the round-lot filter actually has beyond all-lot and subpenny imbalance, and whether round-lot share is stationary across 2015–present — is embedded in the identification stage rather than run as a day-one gate with a pre-committed threshold.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Round-lot trades have declined sharply as a share of prints since 2015 while odd-lot share has risen with price levels, and RLOIB is built from the same signed-trade tape as ALLOIB. If corr(RLOIB, ALLOIB) is ~0.95 in this universe, the residual the whole design rests on is mostly noise, and the entire TAQ build, RETOIB subpenny construction and venue-data validation would have been spent to learn that. The plan proposes residualization but names no variance-retained floor and no coverage/stationarity diagnostic as a stopping point.
issues.what_breaks: Identification step. A near-degenerate residual produces a null at h=1,5,20 that is uninterpretable — indistinguishable from 'no retail information' versus 'no independent variation to test' — after the expensive build is sunk.
issues.fix: Week-one deliverable before RETOIB construction: correlation matrix of RLOIB/ALLOIB/ODDOIB, R² and residual variance share from the residualization, and round-lot share of volume and prints by year × price bucket × size bucket. Pre-commit a residual variance floor (e.g. <15% retained after controls) and a break test on round-lot share as kill/re-scope triggers.

issues.summary: No test of where the mechanism says the signal should be absent: retail-intensity conditioning enters only as a linear institutional-ownership control, not as a negative control.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The claim is specifically that round lots tag retail. The stated mechanism implies near-zero predictability in the names where retail participation is minimal — top-decile institutional ownership, high-priced mega-caps where retail trades odd lots by necessity. The existing placebos (mixed lots, exact-100, forward shift, sign randomization) all test the lot filter and the timing, none tests the retail story. If RLOIB fades returns just as strongly in the lowest-retail quintile, the design as written would still report a t>3 net alpha and attribute it to retail flow when it is generic order-flow reversal or microstructure.
issues.what_breaks: The interpretation attached to the portfolio result, and with it the durability judgement — a generic reversal effect has very different crowding and decay properties than a retail-flow one.
issues.fix: Add a pre-committed cross-sectional negative control: sort on retail intensity (RETOIB volume share, institutional ownership, price level) and require the RLOIB coefficient and net alpha to be monotonically weaker and statistically indistinguishable from zero in the lowest-retail bucket. A uniform effect across retail intensity should be reported as failure of the retail interpretation, not as a stronger result.

issues.summary: Entry timing is left as 't+1' without specifying whether the position is established at the open or the close, and the cost model does not distinguish the two — yet that is where the harvestability answer lives.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Daily-frequency reversal against same-day order-flow imbalance is known to accrue disproportionately overnight and in the first half hour. The signal here is complete at 16:00 on day t. If entry is the t+1 close, most of a real h=1 effect is already gone and the plan will conclude 'unharvestable' about a signal that is harvestable at the open; if entry is the t+1 open, the effective half-spread plus square-root impact model calibrated on continuous-session prints understates auction and opening-minutes cost. This firm has the tick data and in-house execution to resolve it and the plan does not use them.
issues.what_breaks: The portfolio and cost stage, and therefore the headline breakeven-cost output — the central deliverable for this firm.
issues.fix: Decompose the h=1 return into overnight, first 30 minutes, and rest-of-day, and specify entry timestamp explicitly. Cost the open-auction and opening-minutes entry from tick data rather than from a session-average half-spread, and report breakeven cost separately by entry window.

issues.summary: The clause allowing a sign flip at longer horizons to be 'reinterpreted, not failure' leaves the tradeable direction unpinned across three horizons and two regimes.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The information-content falsifier is properly sign-agnostic and pre-committed, which is fine. But the tradeable claim is directional, and the plan gives itself latitude to choose sign and horizon after seeing results across h=1/5/20 in both the pre-2020 and post-2020 subsamples. With a t>3 bar that is survivable, but the split at end-2019 that the plan already builds makes the fix free.
issues.what_breaks: The net-alpha t-statistic in the evaluation stage becomes partly in-sample with respect to sign and horizon choice, which is exactly the thing the research committee will re-run and question.
issues.fix: Fix sign, primary horizon and holding rule on the 2015–2019 half, then report the 2020–present result as a straight out-of-sample read with no re-selection. Report the full sensitivity grid distribution (including worst-case t) alongside the primary spec rather than the primary alone.

issues.summary: Crowding is not addressed, despite being one of the firm's three stated acceptance criteria.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Retail-order-imbalance reversal via subpenny classification is among the most widely published and replicated microstructure signals of the last five years, and the plan uses it as a control — so the team already knows the neighbourhood is populated. The incrementality test versus RETOIB establishes a statistical variant view but says nothing about whether the round-lot variant is itself already in books, nor whether the wholesalers who internalise the profitable retail flow leave only adversely selected residual on the exchange tape as round lots.
issues.what_breaks: Even a clean t>3 net alpha arrives with no read on whether the historical Sharpe is available going forward, which is the question the committee will ask before allocating.
issues.fix: Frame the end-2019 split explicitly as a post-publication decay test with a pre-committed expectation, correlate strategy returns with known reversal and retail-flow factors and with any available crowding proxies, and state the internalisation argument for who is on the other side and what it predicts about sign and concentration.

issues.summary: Outcome space is binary — standalone long-short net alpha clears t>3 or the effect is filed as 'unharvestable' — which for a multi-signal book with in-house execution understates the decision-relevant uses of a real but weakly profitable signal.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Type II is the expensive error here: the firm runs breadth, absorbs false positives across many small bets, and has execution infrastructure that can monetise a retail-flow read without a standalone book. A signal with net alpha t of 2.2 standalone can still add materially as an orthogonal component or as an execution-scheduling overlay (avoid trading into transient retail-driven pressure), and the plan as written would not measure that.
issues.what_breaks: The evaluation stage terminates on a standalone test, so a genuine effect that fails the standalone hurdle produces no usable output despite the data to assess its marginal contribution already being in hand.
issues.fix: Add one step: regress the RLOIB strategy's net returns on the in-house existing signal ensemble to report marginal information ratio, and report the signal's ability to predict same-name transient price pressure at the horizons the execution desk trades over, as a separate deliverable from the standalone alpha.

response.overall: This is a well-matched plan for this firm — right horizon, right acceptance criteria (cost, capacity, breakeven cost as a headline rather than an asserted Sharpe), a genuine pre-committed falsifier that separates 'lot filter adds nothing' from 'real but unharvestable', and it correctly treats the round-lot-equals-retail premise as something to test rather than inherit. The gaps are refinements, not repairs: the cheapest possible kill (does the round-lot residual have any independent variation, and is round-lot share stationary across 2015–present) should be a day-one gate with a numeric threshold rather than buried in the identification stage; there is no mechanism-derived negative control on retail intensity, so a generic reversal effect could be reported as a retail one; and entry timing plus crowding — the two things that actually decide harvestability for this book — are left implicit. Fix those four and it is worth the quarter.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold. Specific and earned: RLOIB and ALLOIB come off the same signed tape, the plan names residualization but no variance-retained floor or coverage/stationarity gate, so a near-degenerate residual would yield an uninterpretable null after the whole TAQ/RETOIB build is sunk. A desk would take the sequencing point seriously.

Not in gold. Checks the plan's actual placebo list (mixed lots, exact-100, forward shift, sign randomization) and correctly notes none tests the retail mechanism; retail intensity enters only as a linear institutional-ownership control. The proposed negative control (low-retail, high-price mega-cap names) is a concrete, plan-specific fix bearing on the interpretation of the portfolio result.

Not in gold, but legitimate and specific: the plan literally says 'signal at t, entry t+1' without specifying open or close, and the half-spread-plus-square-root-impact model is calibrated on continuous-session prints. Given that daily order-flow reversal accrues overnight/early, this materially moves the headline breakeven-cost output.

Not in gold. Quotes the plan's own escape clause ('a positive 20-day coefficient is reinterpreted, not failure') and correctly notes the tradeable claim is directional while sign and horizon remain unpinned across h=1/5/20 and two subsamples. Concrete and cheap to fix with the split the plan already builds.

Not in gold. Earned rather than recited: it uses the plan's own choice of RETOIB as a control to argue the team knows the neighbourhood is populated, and adds a firm-specific mechanism (wholesalers internalising the good retail flow leave adversely selected residual on the exchange tape as round lots) that bears directly on forward availability of the alpha.

The constructive core — the plan's binary standalone t>3 / 'unharvestable' terminus discards information about marginal contribution to a multi-signal book or an execution-scheduling overlay — is a real gap in the evaluation stage. But the stated error-asymmetry rationale sits awkwardly with this firm's context, where the stated killer is quoting into informed flow labelled uninformed (a Type I failure), and the 'firm runs breadth, absorbs false positives' framing reads as generic multi-strategy boilerplate. Escalating rather than calling it manufactured.

response.plan_implied_asker: a microstructure research group at a large systematic equities firm with full TAQ, proprietary exchange feeds and a replication platform
response.what_would_falsify: Pre-committed and explicit: lift <2.0x (or bootstrap LB <1.5x) on Rule 605 accounting / Hui-Walter; recall <35%; signing accuracy <70% (hard stop <60%) vs RLP-flagged known-side prints; mean stock-day r <0.40 vs sub-penny label or <0.25 vs VandaTrack; |t|<3 on round-lot imbalance incremental to Benchmark-A imbalance in the forward-return panel. Author also states H0 as his own prior (round lots are an institutional scheduler signature) and commits to publishing the negative result plus a map of better identifiers.

issues.summary: Five hard gates joined by AND, with thresholds asserted rather than derived from what the signal would need, will kill a usable identifier in a setting where the missed-effect error is the expensive one.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This is a diversified systematic book judged on whether a signal survives costs across ~2,000 names; a false positive dies in the replication platform, a false negative is a permanently forgone sleeve. Yet the design requires G1 AND G2 AND G3 AND G4 AND G5 to pass in a single venue partition, then applies Benjamini-Hochberg on top. Nothing in the plan connects recall ≥35% to tradability: a round-lot filter with 15% recall and 5x lift across 2,000 names produces plenty of signal-days, and 15% recall on an unbiased subsample of retail is a perfectly good instrument. The same is true of the 70% signing floor — 65% signing with 4x lift is economically live.
issues.what_breaks: The Phase 1 → Phase 2 decision. Under conjunctive gating the joint pass probability is far below any individual gate's, so the most likely outcome is a kill that reflects threshold calibration rather than the absence of retail content, and Phase 2 never runs.
issues.fix: Derive the thresholds from economics rather than convention: state, for a given lift/recall/signing triple, the implied information ratio of a round-lot imbalance signal on this universe, and gate on that composite rather than on each component. Replace the AND with a scored decision (e.g. proceed if the implied signal-to-noise clears a stated bar in any partition), and drop BH correction on gates that are already pre-registered and directional — it double-counts conservatism.

issues.summary: G4's r ≥ 0.40 threshold is set against a benchmark whose error rate the plan itself documents, with no attenuation correction, so a perfect identifier could fail it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan states Benchmark A has sign-error rates 'in the tens of percent' and is degraded by midpoint migration — and then requires mean stock-day correlation ≥0.40 against exactly that label. With 20–30% sign errors plus low recall, observed correlation is attenuated well below true agreement; the plan invokes latent-class estimation precisely for this reason at G1 but not at G4. The VandaTrack gate at 0.25 is worse: it is a daily, sample-based, name-limited aggregate correlated against stock-day series.
issues.what_breaks: G4 becomes a coin-flip gate that, under the conjunctive structure of the previous issue, can single-handedly kill the project for measurement reasons rather than economic ones.
issues.fix: Express G4 as noise-corrected agreement (attenuation-corrected r using the label error rates estimated in G1, or a latent-class kappa) and state the threshold in those units. Also front-load the feasibility check the plan flags but does not schedule — confirm the RLP flag exists in historical, not just live, feeds before G3/G4 are designed around it, since both anchors collapse if it does not.

issues.summary: The one test that establishes whether the identification question has any economic stakes (does round-lot imbalance add anything beyond standard order-flow imbalance and existing retail proxies) sits last, behind four label-quality gates.
issues.why_it_applies_here: On this firm's infrastructure the G5 panel — forward returns on Benchmark-A imbalance plus round-lot imbalance with double-clustered SEs — is a couple of days of work on data already licensed, far cheaper than assembling RLP flags across seven venues and running Hui-Walter. The plan's stated reason for deferring it (avoiding a retrofitted retail story) is legitimate but does not require the test to be last, only that its thresholds be pre-registered, which they already are.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of exchange-feed acquisition and label triangulation are spent before knowing whether round-lot imbalance carries any incremental predictive content at all. If it does not, the identification result is a publication, not a trade, and the project should have ended in week one.
issues.fix: Run G5 in parallel with Benchmark C in the first week, with a pre-registered kill: if round-lot imbalance is not incrementally predictive of forward returns net of a standard OFI control, stop — the retail-attribution question is academic for this book. Keep the identification gates as the interpretive layer, not as a prerequisite.

issues.summary: Identification is validated entirely in the pre-half-penny, fixed-100 regime, but any resulting signal would trade under the tiered round-lot definition and the new tick regime.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The sample is deliberately 36 months ending before half-penny compliance because Benchmark A only survives there. But the plan's own H0 turns on retail routing behaviour (dollar/fractional orders arriving as odd lots) and on where the round-lot boundary sits — both of which the amendments change directly. A 100-share threshold that is diagnostic when 100 is the universal round lot means something different when the round lot is 40 or 10 shares at high prices.
issues.what_breaks: Phase 2 signal construction. Gates could pass on a definition of 'round lot' that no longer exists at deployment, and the retail/institutional separation could invert if schedulers re-slice to the new tiers.
issues.fix: Add a post-compliance out-of-time check using Benchmark B alone (RLP flags survive the regime change; sub-penny does not) on a shorter recent window, as a required condition before Phase 2. Report lift/recall/signing under both the fixed-100 and tiered definitions in the recent window, not just the historical one.

issues.summary: G3 measures signing accuracy on RLP-flagged lit executions, a subpopulation that is unrepresentative of where the bulk of retail flow actually prints.
issues.why_it_applies_here: RLP flow is the slice retail brokers route to exchanges rather than sell to wholesalers — a selected residual, and the plan itself says its recall is 'very low'. Most retail volume in this sample period is internalized and prints to the TRF. Signing accuracy estimated on RMO-certified lit prints need not transfer to TRF round lots, yet G3 is one of the two hard stops.
issues.what_breaks: G3 either passes or fails for reasons specific to a small, selected venue population, and that verdict is then applied to the off-exchange partition where the signal would actually live.
issues.fix: Estimate signing accuracy separately within each partition, using the Rule 605 buy/sell composition and latent-class machinery for the TRF partition rather than importing the RLP-derived number; make the hard stop partition-specific and state explicitly which partition the Phase 2 signal would be built in.

issues.summary: Phase 2's go/no-go criteria specify after-cost Sharpe, worst year and net/gross but never state a return horizon, a capacity figure or a crowding check — the three things this firm actually judges signals on.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'Forward returns' in G5 and 'directional continuation' in Phase 2 are left unspecified, and the sign of the trade depends on it: at intraday horizons the economics are liquidity provision against uninformed flow, at weekly horizons the published retail-imbalance effect runs with retail, not against it. The firm's horizon is days to weeks, so the plan must commit to which claim it is testing. Separately, retail concentration is not uniform across the universe, so capacity is the binding question for a flow-inference signal, and the plan's own pitfall about retail drifting toward systematic day-trading is exactly a crowding argument it never tests.
issues.what_breaks: A Phase 2 pass at Sharpe 1.0 with unspecified horizon and no capacity estimate is not a result this committee can act on; net/gross >0.40 constrains cost but says nothing about size.
issues.fix: Pre-specify the horizon grid (e.g. 30min / 1d / 5d / 20d) and state which horizon the mechanism predicts and with what sign. Add a capacity condition to the go/no-go (turnover-scaled notional at which net/gross degrades below 0.40) and a crowding check — correlation of the round-lot imbalance signal with published retail-imbalance and short-term-reversal factors.

response.overall: This is a well-built plan and unusually honest: it separates identification from profitability, states the author's own prior as the null, front-loads a spreadsheet-only test that can kill the project in a week, pre-commits falsifiers, and pairs the one sophisticated method with arithmetic the committee can check. The real risk is not credulity but the opposite — five conjunctive hard gates with thresholds that were asserted rather than derived, one of them uncorrected for label noise the plan itself documents, in a setting where a missed real effect is the expensive error; the most likely outcome as written is a false kill. Recalibrate the gates against implied signal economics, move the incremental-return test to week one alongside Benchmark C, and add a post-compliance RLP-only check so the result transfers to the regime it would trade in.

issue_buckets.why: Same concern as blocking#1 (and overlaps blocking#5): conjunctive kill gates with un-derived thresholds against imperfect labels mean the project dies on threshold calibration rather than economics. The why_it_applies_here misdescribes the firm as a diversified systematic book judged across ~2,000 names, but the objection itself is the reviewer's.

A specific instantiation of blocking#1: G4's 0.40 correlation floor is set against a benchmark whose sign-error rate the plan itself documents, with no attenuation correction, so measurement error is read as signal absence. Correctly earned on this plan's own text (latent-class used at G1 but not G4; VandaTrack aggregate vs stock-day).

Matches blocking#5 — economics/incremental-content test deferred behind label gates — and adds the correct observation that pre-registration, not last position, is what protects against a retrofitted retail story.

Matches blocking#3: the half-penny/tiered-round-lot break is dodged by truncating to a pre-compliance window, so identification is established under a round-lot definition and tick regime that will not exist at deployment.

Not in gold as a distinct item, but a legitimate, plan-specific point: G3 is a hard stop estimated on RMO-certified lit RLP prints — a selected, admittedly very-low-recall residual — while the bulk of retail in this sample internalizes to the TRF, which is the partition where the signal would live. A desk would take the transfer-validity objection seriously.

Rests on a false premise about this firm ('the firm's horizon is days to weeks', weekly retail-imbalance effects), and the capacity/crowding demand is the generic systematic-equity checklist rather than something earned against a nanosecond-to-seconds internalizer whose economics are spread capture net of adverse selection and inventory risk. The kernel that Phase 2 leaves the return horizon unspecified is real, but the objection as written points away from the reviewer's actual horizon complaint.

response.plan_implied_asker: A larger fundamental shop with a multi-analyst deep-dive team and prior-cycle history at hand, able to spend a quarter reconstructing four industry episodes
response.what_would_falsify: Stated negative criteria: negative implied gross bookings two consecutive quarters; channel inventory >1.5x normal; a backlog/LTA definition change in a quarter that would otherwise have declined; supplier finished-goods inventory rising two quarters while backlog is called record. Plus the explicit prior that announcement count alone carries no information.

issues.summary: The decisive, cheap checks are buried inside a large simultaneous pipeline with no stated order or early gate.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Three checks resolve most of this question in days: does the company disclose RPO at all and under what ASC 606 policy; has any customer cash arrived (contract liabilities, deposits, reservation fees, capex funding on the cash flow statement); and what durable horizon is already embedded in EV via reverse DCF. If there is no cash and no minimums, the whole tiering/coverage/backtest apparatus is moot. The plan lists these alongside peer and prior-cycle reconstruction as if equal cost.
issues.what_breaks: One analyst at a five-person shop starts with the RPO roll-forward and prior-cycle calibration and spends weeks before learning whether the commitments are cash-backed — the single fact that determines the answer.
issues.fix: Restate as a gated sequence: Week 1 = RPO policy footnote + customer cash trace + reverse DCF implied horizon. Pre-commit that if no customer cash and no binding minimums appear, the work stops and the answer is 'announcements, not durability.' Everything else is conditional on passing that gate.

issues.summary: The 'LTA-to-RPO gap' is treated as the key signal without first establishing what this company's RPO policy actually excludes.
issues.why_it_applies_here: ASC 606 practical expedients let issuers exclude contracts under one year and variable consideration allocated to wholly unsatisfied performance obligations, and some issuers exclude cancellable amounts entirely. Shortage-era LTAs are frequently indexed-price or cancellable-with-notice, i.e. precisely the population an issuer would exclude. The gap between announced LTA value and RPO would then be a disclosure-policy artifact, not evidence of weak claim strength — and could equally be large for a genuinely strong book. The plan inherits the interpretation from the question without testing it.
issues.what_breaks: The tiering step ('in RPO' is an attribute in five of six tier definitions) and the coverage math both mis-rank claim strength; a strong contract book reads as Tier 3, or a weak one reads as Tier 1 if the issuer happens to include cancellable amounts.
issues.fix: Read the revenue recognition footnote's stated RPO exclusions and practical-expedient elections first, and note any change in that policy across the sample. If the exclusions swallow the LTAs, drop 'RPO inclusion' as a scoring attribute and rely on contract language plus received cash.

issues.summary: Haircut percentages presented to two significant figures but calibrated from realized conversion data that is not externally observable.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Companies do not publish backlog-to-revenue conversion rates or cancellation experience; the 2021–23 semiconductor episode gives at most inferred, company-specific fragments. Yet 90–95%/70%/25–35% multiply directly into coverage, which is then compared to hard gates of ≥60% NTM and ≥40% year-two. A ±15-point uncertainty in the Tier 2 haircut flips the gate.
issues.what_breaks: The threshold test at the end of the plan looks quantitative but its verdict is set by an unverifiable parameter, and the IC cannot inspect the calibration because the underlying data does not exist.
issues.fix: Present coverage as a band across a low/base/high haircut grid and require the constructive/negative conclusion to be invariant across the band. State explicitly where each haircut came from, and where it is judgement rather than calibration.

issues.summary: Net bookings solved as a plug, then cancellations 'backed into' from the same identity — underdetermined, and it drives one of the four kill criteria.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The roll-forward has one equation and several unobservables: FX, M&A, contract modifications, reallocation between the 12-month and remainder buckets, and policy-driven exclusions all land in the same residual. Unless the company separately discloses bookings or book-to-bill, 'negative implied gross bookings' can be produced by a modification or an FX swing rather than hidden cancellations — and it is a pre-committed negative criterion, so a spurious firing kills a position.
issues.what_breaks: The negative-criteria gate rejects on an artifact; conversely a real cancellation wave is masked by an offsetting M&A addition.
issues.fix: Only use this criterion where bookings or book-to-bill is independently disclosed. Otherwise reduce it to a flag that triggers a transcript/footnote hunt for the explanation, not an automatic negative.

issues.summary: RPO trajectory cannot be reconstructed for two of the four backtest episodes, and the backtest as scoped is a quarter of analyst time.
issues.why_it_applies_here: ASC 606 RPO disclosure begins in 2018–19; telecom 2000 and memory/passives 2017–18 have no RPO to trace, only company-defined Item 101 backlog with no comparability. The plan's stated backtest output — 'RPO trajectory, realized vs implied coverage' — is unobtainable there. Meanwhile reconstructing four episodes plus peers plus customer mirror tables is not a one-analyst task at a shop with two analysts covering 25–30 names.
issues.what_breaks: Either the analyst burns weeks and returns a backlog-only comparison mislabelled as coverage evidence, or the backtest is quietly abandoned and the haircuts lose the only calibration they claimed.
issues.fix: Cut the backtest to 2021–22 semiconductors plus the live AI-cycle names where RPO exists, and reframe the pre-2018 episodes as qualitative base rates on backlog conversion and pricing rolloff only. Cap the whole exercise at a stated number of analyst-days.

issues.summary: Two mandatory constructive conditions may be structurally unobservable, so the gate can auto-fail a genuinely good situation.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Customers' purchase-obligation tables are aggregate and do not name suppliers, so 'mirror disclosures reconciling to ≥50%' is only measurable when a customer separately names this company in a release or 8-K — often not the case. Segment-level coverage requires RPO or LTA value allocated by product line, which issuers rarely disclose, forcing analyst allocation into a threshold test. Requiring all six conditions makes any single unobservable condition a rejection.
issues.what_breaks: The threshold step returns 'not constructive' for reasons of disclosure availability rather than business quality — a false negative dressed as discipline — or the analyst fills the gap with an allocation assumption and the gate becomes self-fulfilling.
issues.fix: Split the six conditions into must-haves that are always observable (cash support, contract language on minimums and take-or-pay, top-3 concentration, implied-vs-modeled horizon) and corroborators used when available (mirror reconciliation, segment split). State that missing corroborators widen the required margin on the must-haves rather than triggering rejection.

response.overall: The economics here are unusually well thought through for this asset class: it separates announced commitment from enforceable commitment, insists on customer cash as the real test, prices the residue against market-implied durability, and pre-commits four falsifiers plus a correct warning that duration without growth is a downgrade. The problems are ordering and scale, not thinking — the two facts that decide the question (what the company's RPO actually excludes, and whether any customer cash has arrived) sit inside a pipeline that also asks one analyst to rebuild four industry cycles, two of which predate the disclosure the method depends on, and the hard coverage gates are driven by haircuts no external data can calibrate to the precision quoted. Reorder into a one-week gate — RPO policy footnote, contract-liability/deposit trace, reverse DCF implied horizon — run the full register and tiering only if cash and minimums are actually there, and show coverage as a band rather than a point against a 60% line.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold. Legitimate and earned against this firm specifically: one analyst, no infrastructure, and the plan enumerates a customer-cash check (contract liabilities, deposits, capex funding) and a reverse DCF alongside multi-episode prior-cycle reconstruction as if equal cost. The 'if there is no cash and no minimums, the tiering apparatus is moot' gate is a real sequencing observation about this plan's own stated prior (enforceable cash-backed commitment is usually weak), not a generic 'do it in stages' complaint.

Not in gold and not generic. It engages the specific ASC 606-10-50-13 machinery the plan names: practical expedients for sub-one-year contracts and wholly unsatisfied variable consideration, plus issuer discretion on cancellable amounts, mean the LTA-to-RPO gap the plan calls 'the key signal' can be a disclosure-policy artifact. 'In RPO' appears in the tier definitions, so the point bites on the mechanism. A desk would take this seriously.

Same concern as gold secondary#2 (the 90-95/70/25-35 haircuts and the 60%/40% gates are asserted rather than derived, and the verdict is set by an uninspectable parameter), and it overlaps gold blocking#3 on the thinness of the calibration source. The added 'IC cannot inspect the calibration' framing is the same objection dressed for this firm.

Not in gold. Specific to the plan's own stated identity: net bookings solved as a plug and cancellations backed out of the same equation, with FX, M&A, modifications and 12-month/remainder reallocation all landing in one residual — and 'negative implied gross bookings two straight quarters' is a pre-committed kill criterion. That is a genuine underdetermination critique of a named mechanism, not a recited overfitting concern.

Carries gold blocking#3's substance: the backtest that was supposed to calibrate the haircuts cannot deliver for two of the four named episodes, collapsing the calibration base. The added feasibility limb (four episodes plus peers plus customer mirror tables is not one-analyst work at a two-analyst shop covering 25-30 names) is a legitimate firm-fit extension rather than a separate manufactured point.

Adjacent to gold secondary#2 but a distinct objection: not that the thresholds are underived, but that two of them are structurally unobservable — customer purchase-obligation tables are aggregate and do not name suppliers, and segment-level RPO/LTA allocation is rarely disclosed — so an all-six conjunctive gate auto-fails on disclosure availability rather than business quality. Earned from the actual disclosure regime, not recited.

response.plan_implied_asker: A multi-analyst macro/commodity research shop with standing subscriptions to industrial price series, customs data and a dedicated cross-cycle historian
response.what_would_falsify: Episodes where contracted price stayed materially above spot for 8+ quarters after supply normalization in the absence of a hard qualification moat — that would break the "honored in volume, broken in price, split by switching cost" thesis. Plus pre-registered HBM checks (contract-liability direction, RPO growth threshold, customs shipments, customer obligation tables) resolvable within 12 months.

issues.summary: The plan builds a cross-industry framework and never applies it to the company that prompted the question.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The question is whether THIS name's shortage guidance implies durable revenue. Every data item listed — supplier 10-Ks, customer obligation tables, price series — is scoped to the 20-30 analog episodes. No step establishes the subject's requalification lag, whether its parts are single-sourced mid-program or fungible, what its RPO and contract-liability lines currently say, what its customers' purchase-obligation tables show, or how its LTA book behaved in its own prior cycle. The plan's own thesis says the switching cost, not the label, is the variable — so the subject's placement on that axis is the whole answer, and it is the one thing not measured.
issues.what_breaks: Step 4-6 produce base rates and a capacity ledger for other markets; the output ('probability-weighted haircut') then has to be assigned to the name by assertion. If the subject sits at the aerospace-forging end, the entire fragility thesis is irrelevant to it; if at the container end, most of the episode work was unnecessary.
issues.fix: Add as step 0, before any episode work: determine the subject's qualification lag and alternate-source availability from customer engineering disclosures and its own filings; pull its RPO/contract-liability and top customers' purchase-obligation tables for this cycle and the prior one; document how its last cycle's commitments resolved. If the subject has a prior comparable shortage, that record outranks any cross-industry base rate and should be the primary evidence.

issues.summary: Scale and data spend are not executable by one analyst at a five-person shop and are committed before any cheap test.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Twenty-five to thirty episodes coded on ten contract features across three outcome dates, plus Exhibit 10 contract reading, plus PACER/Chancery/ICC/SIAC/foreign court dockets, plus per-market capacity ledgers with ramp curves and hidden capacity, requires TrendForce, Fastmarkets, Benchmark, UxC, Argus/ICIS, Drewry/Xeneta, Panjiva or ImportGenius and the SEMI fab database. That is a six-figure data bill and multiple analyst-quarters at a shop with two analysts, no engineers, and nobody who maintains a database. Neither the capacity ledger nor the customs reconciliation is maintainable in Excel over a 3-5 year hold.
issues.what_breaks: The work either stalls partway with an incomplete episode set — at which point the base rates are whatever subset got finished, i.e. worse than no base rate — or consumes the analyst for a quarter on a position decision that has to be made now.
issues.fix: Cheap version, one analyst, 2-3 weeks, no new licences: (a) the subject-specific work in issue 1; (b) three analog episodes chosen for closest qualification profile to the subject, not the widest spread — read the actual contract exhibits and trace price and volume for eight quarters past the peak using Bloomberg series already on the terminal; (c) one page on what the current multiple embeds about duration. Commission the wider episode study only if (b) shows the subject's category is genuinely ambiguous.

issues.summary: Both validation tests are circular: the holdout outcome is already known and cited in the plan, and the negative-control test re-derives the criterion the cases were selected on.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan proposes holding out the 2021-2024 auto-semi cycle and predicting outcomes 'before checking' — while itself already citing the ~$16bn LTSA figure, the Renesas-Wolfspeed deposit, and 'the 2023-2025 correction.' The outcome is in the analyst's head. Separately, aerospace forgings are labelled 'best case: hold' and MLCC/containers 'worst case' in the episode list, and then the stated validation is 'test that aerospace/LNG score durable and MLCC/containers fragile.' A framework built to explain outcome-labelled cases will reproduce those labels by construction.
issues.what_breaks: The validation step produces a pass regardless of whether the switching-cost mechanism has any predictive content, and the IC will be shown a framework certified by a test it could not fail.
issues.fix: Drop the auto-semi holdout and rely on the live HBM pre-registration, which is genuinely out-of-sample — but recognise it resolves after the decision. For the historical work, replace validation-by-reproduction with a blind step: have the second analyst score qualification lag and sourcing for each episode from pre-normalization filings only, with outcome data withheld, then compare rankings to realised outcomes.

issues.summary: Conditional base rates rest on an outcome-bracketed, cycle-clustered sample; the probability weights will not survive scrutiny.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The episode list was assembled by naming known cases to span a range ('best case', 'worst case', 'upper bound'), so unconditional frequencies from it are not base rates. And the episodes are not independent draws: containers 2021-23, ABF 2021-23, auto semis 2021-24, lithium 2022-24 and HBM 2023-26 are largely one post-COVID demand shock; MLCC 2017-19, DRAM/NAND 2017-19 and lithium 2017-20 are largely another. Effective N is three or four shocks, not thirty. Conditioning on qualification lag × sourcing × credit × pricing then leaves cells of one or two. The plan's own pitfall list names demand-driven-shortage vs supply-shock-in-flat-demand as 'likely the dominant variance driver' but no design step separates them.
issues.what_breaks: Step 4 and the 'probability-weighted haircut' output attach numerical probabilities to cells with n≈2 drawn from a sample chosen to bracket outcomes. An IC that spots this discards the whole exercise.
issues.fix: Keep the ranking, drop the probabilities. Present as an ordered set of named case comparisons with the subject placed between the two nearest analogs, and state the sample was chosen for range rather than representativeness. Cluster episodes by macro shock and report whether the switching-cost ordering holds within each shock separately.

issues.summary: The step that could resolve the question in days sits behind a multi-quarter pipeline, and nothing is actionable before the position decision.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The thesis is explicitly bimodal on one variable — in-term requalification feasibility. For a single name that is a days-long determination from teardown reports, customer qualification disclosures and one or two industry calls. Placing it nowhere while episode coding, capacity ledgers and breach arithmetic run first means the analyst learns the answer's category last, and the HBM pre-registration checks resolve in twelve months against guidance that lands next quarter.
issues.what_breaks: By the time steps 5-6 finish, the guidance has been either confirmed or broken by reported results and the multiple has re-rated either way.
issues.fix: Sequence: subject qualification lag → subject and customer contract disclosures → nearest three analogs → only then broader base rates and capacity ledger, and only if the subject is genuinely ambiguous. Commit up front to what the analyst tells the IC in three weeks.

response.overall: The analytical core is unusually good: a real variant view stated against what the market is paying for, a genuine falsifier, negative controls derived from the mechanism, ranked rather than regressed inference, and a haircut rather than a fabricated P&L — all of which suits a sceptical IC. But it is written for a research shop three times this size, and it never actually analyses the company that prompted the question: the one determination that decides the answer, whether the subject's product can be requalified in-term, appears nowhere. Send it back scoped to the subject plus three closest analogs, using data already on the terminal, and drop the probability weights and the self-confirming validation.

issue_buckets.why: Legitimate and specific to this plan: the seed question is about one name, the plan's own thesis makes the subject's requalification lag/single-sourcing the decisive variable, and no step measures it for the subject. The output would be assigned to the company by assertion. Not in gold, but a desk would take it seriously.

Same concern as gold blocking#1 — the plan is built on vendor datasets and infrastructure this five-person, no-engineer shop cannot buy or operate, and commits the analyst before any cheap test. Adds the execution-scale angle but the core is the reviewer's data-constraint objection.

Earned and plan-specific: the plan cites the ~$16bn LTSA figure, the Renesas-Wolfspeed deposit and 'the 2023-2025 correction' while proposing to hold out that same cycle, and pre-labels aerospace/LNG 'best case' and MLCC/containers 'worst case' before declaring the validation to be that aerospace/LNG score durable and MLCC/containers fragile. That is a concrete circularity in the stated validation, not a recited canonical objection.

The dominant thrust — effective N is three or four correlated shocks rather than thirty, and conditioning on qualification lag x sourcing x credit x pricing leaves cells of one or two so probabilities are unsupported — is precisely the 'twenty to thirty episodes is too few or too heterogeneous' objection the reviewer explicitly ruled out, noting the plan ranks by conditional base rate rather than regressing and within-industry behavior is stable across cycles once cause and regime are accounted for. Flagged uncertain because the accompanying outcome-bracketed-selection point (episodes chosen to span 'best case'/'worst case', so unconditional frequencies are not base rates) is a distinct objection the reviewer did not address; if scored alone it would be real_unlisted.

Sharp sequencing point tied to this plan and firm: the thesis is bimodal on one determinable variable, the subject's in-term requalification feasibility, which an analyst could settle in days, yet it sits behind episode coding, capacity ledgers and breach arithmetic, and the HBM pre-registration checks resolve in twelve months against a decision due now. Not in gold and not a generic recitation.

response.plan_implied_asker: A concentrated fundamental long-only shop doing filings-and-Excel work on one holding, where being wrong about the cost base is the risk that matters
response.what_would_falsify: Reconciled spend plus the inverted sensitivity showing that the uplift required to breach the guided margin floor or miss consensus by 2% is far above any plausible vendor increase — i.e. total impact under ~25bps — at which point tone is declared uninformative and the hypothesis is dropped (with a separately logged, non-thesis open question).

issues.summary: The comparable-customer uplift distribution that produces the 'central case' — the number that triggers the call — cannot actually be observed, so percentile precision is manufactured.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Enterprise licence renewal uplifts for named customers are essentially never disclosed by either party. Step 3 proposes a median/75th/90th percentile from 5–10 comparables built out of vendor NRR, RPO-vs-billings and analyst-firm commentary. NRR blends seat expansion, cross-sell and price across the whole book; RPO versus billings does not cleanly separate price from volume for one contract. The plan then feeds this fabricated distribution into a decision rule ('central case over ~75bps forces a call') and pre-states 15–30% in the hypothesis before any work, so the anchor is set before evidence.
issues.what_breaks: Step 3 and the comparison in Step 5 ('compare to Step 3's distribution'). The whole call ends up resting on a judgment dressed as an estimated percentile, and the IC cannot distinguish the two. The 75th-percentile-as-median adjustment compounds an invented number rather than correcting it.
issues.fix: Drop the percentile framing entirely. Keep only the inversion: solve for the uplift required to breach the guided floor / miss consensus by 2%, then ask a small number of checkable questions — what has the vendor's published list price done over three years, what did this company's own last two renewals do to the line, what does an ex-procurement or SAM consultant say the vendor is asking of similar accounts. Present the uplift as a bounded judgment with named sources, not a distribution.

issues.summary: Step 2 — self-declared the highest-priority input — names sources that will not contain the information: a vendor licence is not filed as a material contract by the customer.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan correctly identifies metric changes (per-server to per-core, bundling, audit settlement) as where the step-function tail lives, and says that is the highest priority. But it proposes to find price-protection caps, true-up rights, MFN and audit clauses in material-contract exhibits and prior 8-Ks. Ordinary-course vendor agreements are not material to a $400M-cap-relevant customer and are not filed; risk factors will be generic. The one party who knows is management, and management is the reason for the question.
issues.what_breaks: Step 2 returns nothing on the specific negotiated terms, so the metric-change scenario in Step 5 gets populated with assumptions and then quoted in bps as though modelled. The tail case — the only branch that is thesis-relevant for a 3–5 year holder — becomes the least evidenced part of the output.
issues.fix: Name the sources that do exist: the vendor's published licensing rulebook and price list (these are public for the major enterprise vendors and define what metric shifts are even possible), one expert-network call with an ex-procurement/SAM person on that vendor's current playbook, and a direct IR question on the licensing metric basis and whether price protection survives the new term. If none of these resolve it, say so and carry the metric-change tail as an unquantified position-risk question rather than a bps figure.

issues.summary: The cheapest test of whether public data can answer the question at all — can the last renewal be seen in the reported expense lines — sits in Step 4 and in validation, behind the sizing and mechanics work.
issues.why_it_applies_here: On the plan's own hypothesis the licence is mid-single-digit percent of opex and a 15–30% uplift phases over years. That is very likely below the visible noise in a reported opex line. If the prior renewal produced no detectable inflection over four quarters, the back-test proposed under Validation ('predicts the realized move within error bars') cannot be run — and that finding also tells you the current renewal will not be observable ex post either, which changes what the work can deliver.
issues.what_breaks: The single named validation step may be unexecutable, discovered only after Steps 1–3 are sunk. The plan would then have a sensitivity table with no external calibration and no stated fallback.
issues.fix: Run the detectability check immediately after top-down sizing: pull the last two renewal dates and look at the relevant expense line for four quarters after each. If nothing is visible, stop calling it a back-test, state that ex-post confirmation is unavailable, and shift the standard to internal consistency (top-down/bottom-up reconciliation plus the inversion) declared up front.

issues.summary: Scope is disproportionate to the stated base case, and the expensive stages are not gated on the branch that would justify them.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself concludes the base case is 30–90bps — 'material to a quarter, not the thesis' — for a manager holding three to five years. Against that, GSA/Crown Commercial schedule triangulation, LinkedIn headcount reconstruction, RFP postings, migration NPV with integration-points costing, and covenant headroom are several analyst-weeks out of a two-analyst shop. Covenant headroom in particular only matters if the impact is an order of magnitude above the hypothesised range.
issues.what_breaks: Analyst time is the binding constraint here, not compute. The plan spends it uniformly across branches rather than concentrating it where the answer changes the position.
issues.fix: Make the branch explicit: Days 1–3 are purchase obligations plus segment opex to bound spend, single-source yes/no, and the inversion for required uplift. Only if the required uplift falls inside plausible vendor behaviour, or the vendor is single-source with a live metric-change route, do Steps 3–5 in full. Drop covenant headroom and migration NPV from the base path.
